ILLUSTRAIED FASHIONS.

Muslin gowns this summer have achieved the -acme of beauty in colouring and texture, and the prices are so exceedingly moderate, that it is within the power of every one to possess themselves of a pretty and dainty dress for sunny days. Indeed, every ensuing season the materials turned out by the manufacturers seem more beautiful than ever both as regards colouring and design, till their fascinations are almost bewildering. Perfectly pure white gowns will be much in evidence this season, and look most charming when expressed in spotted or clear muslin or in the newest soft silky- surfaced linen. Never were silks, taffetas, linens, and laces so alluring as now, and also never may it be said were they so cheap or in such variety as regards both pattern and style. A happy cons.

IMPORTANT TO MILK SELLERS. Warrington Magistrates and the Corporation. A decision of considerable interest to milk-sellers was given by the magistrates, (Mr F Mooks presiding), at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, when William Thomas Shutt, of Albert-street, was summoned for wilfully abstracting a certain percentage of cream from milk which he offered for sale. Mr Stanley Wilson, deputy town cierk, appeared for the Corporation, who prosecuted, and the defendant was represented by Mr Brow ne. Mr Browne said the case was of the utmost import- ance to the persons he represented—the milk dealers. Mr Flood, the inspector of nuisances, took a sample of milk from the defendant for the purpose of analysis, and divith dlt as usual, and afterwards defendant re- ceived a summcns under an Act of Parliament passed only a year ago' charging him with abstracting cream from the milk. It was necessary for the Corporation to prove the abstraction. The cream was not seen to be abstracted. When the summons was issued he (Mr Browne) advised that defendant's sample should be analyzed. Dr. Gornall's certificate of analy- sis stated that the percentage of fat was 2.07, whereas the Board of Agricnlure tin their wisdom said it should not be less than three. Defend- ant's sample was analyzed by one of the leading firms in England and was found to be within the limit of 3 per cent. They were going to issue a summons to their analyst to attend court when they received notice by telephone from the Corporation that the summons upon defendant was withdrawn. He therefore asked that the Corporation should be called upon to pay the costs that had been incurred by defendant. In this case the Cor- poration should be looked upon as an absolutely inde- pendent party. If they issued a summons after due Sonsideration, and afterwards when they discovered certain things withdrew it, they should take the conse- quences. If the case were in the High Court or County, Court costs would follow as a matter of course. Defend- ant was in a postien to prove that no cream had been abstracted from the milk, because he had also bad analyzed a quantity of milk from the cow. In this ease it was the cow, and not the man who should have been summoned, because the cow gave poor milk. Defendant had not only been vilified, but had gone to considerable expense, and was entitled to substantial costs. Mr Wilson submitted that if any costs were to be allowed they should he allowed to the Corporation. Ihe sample was taken on June 10th. The analyst gave a certificate on the 13th. It stated that instead of 3 per cent of fat there was only 2'07. On June 15th, at the request of the Milk Dealers' Association, a sample of milk was taken from the farmer's cart. That was analyzed and came out much the same as that obtained from the milk-seller. The public analyst was not satis- fied, and upon his instructicn the Inspector obtained a sample of milk from the cow. The analysis of that re- , suited much the same as in the other cases. The ' standard required, however.was 3 per cent and the onus of proof as to whether it was less or not rested with the defendant. Mr Browne said that was not so. It was so under the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, but not under this one. Mr Wilson said the summons had been taken out ureter section aof the Sale of Food and Drugs Act of 1275, and under that Act the onus of proof that cream bad not been obstracted from the milk rested with the person from whom it was purchased. The Corporation had gone cut of their way to do justice to the defendant and should be allowed expenses for their trouble and annoyance. Mr Browne said the further analyses had Peen taken to move that the cream had been ab•tracted, and now it could not be proved. Mr Wilson said they wanted to do the defendant jus- tice. If the case bad been krougbt forward on the first analysis the magistrates would have been bound to con- vict.

Mr Browne said he had an analysis to the contrary.He added that milk was always poorer during June thaa at any other time. The Chairman, after consultation with the other magistrates, said the ease was important, beeause it was the milk-sellers against the Corporation, and the Corporation against the milk-sellers. The magistrates were anxions to settle the matter on a fair basis. He asked Mr Wilson whether it was not considered that three per cent, was rather high. Mr Browne : That is exactly what the milk-sellers say. Mr Wilson said the staneard was set by law, and they had to work by it. The Chairman : It doesn't follow that we should be unjust. Mr Wileon : That is `the reason the case has been I withdrawn. The Chairman : The Corporation have done their 1 duty. It is the Act that is at fault. Mr Browne : It is very hard upen the milk-sellers. During a further consultation among the magis- trates. Mr Browne observed that Mr Wilson had just held out a threat that it costa were granted aeainst the Corpora- tion another summons would he issued to-morrow. Mr Wilson said he had not made any threat and Mr Browne's remark was molt unfair and unprofessional. Mr Browne: This is a case of petty spite. The Chairman said the summons would be with- drawn, upon the ayment of 20s costs by the Corpora- tion.

Mr Wi!son said ths summons was issued before the second sample was trken. The Chairman replied that his answer to that was that the Corporation Phnuld be extremely careful before they issued any summer!,

div.head: PRETTY TOILETTE.
div.p: A PRETTY TOILETTE.

promise between the airy gossamer fabrics and the heavier materials is given in the dainty toilette illustrated. It is of creamy white nun's veiling* trimmed with guipure lace a a rather greyish tint, commonly termed "twine-coloured." The style is at once simple and smart, which is the aim of the most refined followers of fashion.

Some of the smartest blouses and bodices rt present are made with elbow sleeves, a full frill of lace generally depending from immediately below the elbow, where the sleeve ceases. For outdoors to cover the arms from the elbow long suede gloves of soft tan shades are in vogue, and are very be- coming, while certain soft tones of grey are also much in favour, and harmonize well with some toilettes. Two or three buttons are, of course, per- fectly useless, and hence the re-introduction of the long mousquetaire ankle. Some have suede or kid for the hand part, with lace continued up to the elbow, while others, which are also exceedingly pretty and fashionable, are inlet with lace medallions on the outside of the arm. A very picturesque and quaint revival of a pretty old fashion is to be found in the lace mittens, which are worn with the elbow gauntleted sleeves, which give very much the ap- pearance of a tight fitting continued lace sleeve. There is a marked tendency towards gloves with gauntlets made in every tone of tan and grey kid, while cream doeskin will also be worn. Another somewhat quaint revival is shown by a series of coloured kid tucks on the wrists by four button gloves. White kid gloves have the wrist part comprised of alternate narrow tucks of white and blue or green blue kid.
The shoulder cape sketched is of white chiffon. covered in tiny pin spots in black. The edges of the frills are trimmed with narrow black Valen- ciennes lace edging. These neck ruffles (as triey

div.head: NEW SHOULDER CAPE.
div.p: A NEW SHOULDER CAPE.

used to be called) seem to be a necessary complement so a really dressy toilette, but they should not be affected by a short necked stout woman whose appearance they wilt only effectually mar. A tall woman to whom nature has not been liberal in the matter of flesh is, on the other hand, much improved by the addition of one of these smart capes whose fluffy frills and flowing streamers fill up the figure and softens up any angularities of form. The long flowing, ends are in nearly every instance composed of kilted chiffon. Narrow satin ribbon is often used as a trimming, while little lace or silk appliques or small petalled flowers are intermingled with the lace, silk, net or chiffon of which these dainty complements of the toilette are composed. Parasols and en-tout-car are now much in request. The newest parasols are very dome shaped, which somehow has the effect of making them appear smaller than they really are. The prettiest samples are lined with drawn chiffon, while the outside cover of satin is rendered as beautiful as a flower by numerous frills of chiffon or lace. A charming specimen made for one of this season's brides was of blush pink satin lined with drawn ivory chiffon, the outside being covered with alternate frills of chiffon and lace, the chiffon frills being edged by a ruching of tiny pink Banksian roses, a small cluster of which, with birds and foliage, was fastened to the white enamelled crystal handled stick by narrow pink ribbons.
The summer gown whose charms are depicted is of pale pink batiste with a deep flounce of embroidery at the hem while narrow lines of the same embroidery ornament the top of the flounce.

div.head: SUMMER GOWN.
div.p: A SUMMER GOWN.

and form a finish to the dainty unlined yoke which is of drawn net studded here t.nd there with raised embroidered flowefs. This is a very dainty toilette and a serviceable one withal, for batiste washes well, and the lasting qualities of embroidery are known to all. Lace is lighter looking but will not stand such hard wear as embroidery. A pretty short chine silk sunshade would go well with this dress, especially if it possessed a border in black hair-pin stitch. The handles of both en•towt-car and sunshades are of an ornate description this season, some of the prettiest showing an enamelled stick finishing in a clear crystal ball covered with a fine net work of gold, while a little gold chain replaces the cord and tassels of previous years. One (or more) dainty charm depends from the gold chain, and those can be varied to suit the dress. COQIJETTA

div.head: FATAL FALLS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FATAL FALLS AT WARRINGTON.

An inquest was held at Warrington on Saturday, relative to the death of Isaac Smith, fustian cutter, 16, Dial-court, who fell over the banisters at his house early an Friday morning. Deceased, who was 73 years of age retired to bed under the influence of drink, and getting up at one o'clock in the morning, ever-balanced him- self. Be was dead when picked up. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. _ . .

The circumstances attending the death of Mary Ana Yale, 83 years of age, an inmate of the Workhouse Infirmary, were also inquired into.—Deceased was walk- in gin one of tire wards on May 24th, and fell down fracturing her thigh. She diPd last Friday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. A DELAPIDATED HANDRAIL AT THE SANITARY

div.head: 1:3-ii0-T.----YITAL ACCIDENT.
div.p: 1:3-ii0-T.----YITAL ACCIDENT.

At the Warrington Coronet's Court on Saturday, Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, conducted an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Frederick Ryder, who sustained injuries at the Corporation mini. Lary deT ot, on Tuesday morning, the 24th June, and whieh proved fatal on the following day. Mr Unsworth appeared on behalf of Mr Edward Isherwood,contractor, by whom the deceased was employed ; Mr Crompton (Browne and Crompton) for tbe relatives ; and Mr Horrabin for Mr Deas, engineer to the Corporation,— At the outset a juryman pointea out that the spot where the deceased fell was protected to a height of only nine inches.—Mr Herrabin said the protection was a foot high and added that a factOry inspector paid periodical visits to the works, but he had never drawn their attention to the matter.—Nancy Ryder, wife of the deceased, said her husband was a carter in the employ of Mr Isherwood, and was 27 years of age. She saw him in the Infirmary, but he was unable to tell her how the accident happened.- -Ezra Dutton, labourer, said that on Tuesday morning I the deceased brought a load of refuse to the destructor I house. Witvesa saw him removing the Rhea from the cart, and a rainute;later he rnissed him, subsequently finding him lying in the fire hole. The protection was about a foot high.—The Coroner : Why should it not be higher ?—Witness said it was formerly fire feet high, but it was knocked down by a van about three years ago. A juryman said a portion of a handrail remained,but.it was in such a dilapidated condition that a child falling against it would Cause it to collapse--Nurse Oldrisyd stated that death was due to a fracture of the skull.— , The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and I presented that the death encurred in consequence of the I Corporation neglecting tu keep a proper fence between I the tip stage and the opening into which the deceased I fell.

A Paris correspondent says that Signor Leoncavalle, the Italian composer, is collaborating with the Emperor William in an opera which is to be brought out in Ber- lin next winter, but that the musician is so harassed with telegrams from the Imperial ;ibrettist that be has fled from Paris to an obscure part of Italy, beyond the reach of a telegraph wire.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Since the King was so suddenly stricken down, the superstitious beliefs about the Royal Family have taken an extraordinary hold upon the popular mind. Even people usually credited with a large measure ef common sense have given way to it, and in the shops and in the trains one bears all the old stories repeated, such as that of the gipsy who told Her Majesty that though she would be Queen she would never be crowned. Some point triumphantly to the prophetic atmanacks, others to the soothsayers, and the Paris correspondent of the " Times " was so impressed with these stories that be reperted an interview with Madame de Thebes, a fortune teller, wh3 claims to have predicted the King's illnev, and the nature of Room° eight Or ten years ago. We, of course, hear of many more predietions than were ever made under the circumstances claimed for them, and th 3 worst of it is that those people who repeat them are not in the least disconcerted when these doleful prophecies are falsified by the event. No one we may be sure, will ever be able to reckon up the full extent of the losses involved by the total disloeation of the Coronation arrangements. The pre- peratkons had been so widespread not only in city, town and country, but throughout the Empire, and altogether the total expenditure must have been enormous. In London alone it is said that over a quarter of a million was swallowed up in the timber used for the erection of seats and hoardings, and, in addition to this, and the wasted decorations, there is the loss occasioned by the wholesale abandonment at social engagements. The receipts of the Opera Syndicate for the great gala night were about £25,000, but that is but a small part of the loss since the abandonment of the performance also meant the cancelling of orders to dressmakers, and jewellers, and a cessation of entertaining at dinner parties. The recent terrible strain upon all prominent members of the Royal family, has of course, Yellen heavily upon the Duke of Connaught, the King's only brother,but de- spite his onerous duties he continues to look particularly well, and in the present happe state of affairs, very cheerful. The Duchess too, has done much to relieve the Queen, and the Princess of Wales, and in that sweet gracious way which endears her to all with whom she comes in contact. Her Royal Highness's two daughters, Princess Margaret now in her 21st year. and Princess Victoria Patricia, who is in her seventeenth year, take after the Duchess very much, both in manners and appearance, and are exceedingly charming girls. Ph6tography, as a fashionable! amusement seems to have lost acme of its popularity amongst Society people. They have more recently taken up with the cinemato- graph, with its more entertaining displays. But with the general public, phetoeraphy has lost none of its attractions, and thousands were looking forward to taking Coronation pictures when all the sight peeing and rejoicings were suddenly suspended. Certainly with the aid of photography, the bioscope and other modern inventions, future generations will be much more for- tunate in possessing records of the great events of our time, than we are with regard to the past. Tte &tie- matograpb,with the apparatus for displaying the views, can now be had for about £6or £B, and bow interest-
ing it would be if cnly we bad such a representation say of the Coronation of Queen Elizabeth. That women dress with much better taste than

--- formerly has long teen obvious te the most casual otserver. The short stout woman decked out in a gown of horizontal lines, or the tall thin figureless dam- sel in a tailormach costume,are spectacles now not often seen. But though there has teen a great improvement in popular notions of dress,we have certainly something to learn from French and American women, in the air and manner of bolding ourselves at home, and in our wa!bs abrrad. One vet; a number of American and • ''

Continental women in the park, as well as at other public gatherings, and it is nearly always easy to dis- tinguish them by their carriage, and manner of bolding their skirt which, when not over exaggerated, contri- but-s so largely to that indefinable air of good taste, which is so much to be desired. Speaking generally we are rather disposed to neglect the question of deport- ment, without which even the best dressed woman and the prefessiocal beauty becomes quite unattractive. The array of white, or light toilettes, which appeared with our first glimpse of the summer sun, was positively staitilng. We had grown so accustomed to costumes suitable for wintry weather, that the possibility of summer gowns Ix Mg worn at all this year came as a shock. However, we are rapidly getting over this, and are rejoicing in the eelightfcl change. Unquestionably soft white, unadorned, is thG smartest wear, but if colour is introduced this is of an emerald green shade. The hat to be worn with eitheegown,should be in soft white, draped with black lace, and adorned with sweep- ing Hack and white ostrich plumes. Fr those in deep mourning, wide bandeaux of jet, with eutstanding rosettes of curling jet ribbons, set at the side or at the back, are to be had at all the best shcpa, while for those whose mourning is slightened, these dainty little adornments are edged with steel, which gives the appearance of a tiny piping. Rows of imitation pestle, about the throat or coc sage, are not to be t taught of for a moment, their appearance spelling ruin to tee nicest gown. Women who do not possess bee uttful jewelled collars, v culd do well to pin their I faith to the above Remo, cr failing these, a plain band of
black velvet fastened by a diamond or pearl clasp,or old fashioned brooch, showing stones which in colour match the gown. Tbat the somewhat slipshod white pique riding jacket

_ should have appeared again this year, must be s' atter for regret among smart habit makers. It is, however. much cooler wear and a boon to the woman possessed of an indifferena figure. Not a few daring spirits are too, abandoning the ugly, and usually unbecoming low hat. wearing in its stead a plain neat-looking straw, adorned by a simple band of ribbon—what our grandmothers would have said to such innovations we can well imagine, but after all, it is better perhaps to saCrifice appearance to comfort sometimes. In Paris, the leadersof fashion have taken to reversing the order of writing, in addressing their letters. Instead of the usual style they commence with the name of the town and on the neat line the name and number of the street, and lastly the name of the addressee. It is only one of fashion's freaks, but, though originating in frivolity, it has some sense, as the letter-sorters work would no doubt be facllitated, if this mode of addressing envelopes became the invariable rule. As a matter of fact it is the common way in Esstern Europe of address- ing letters, but it is scarcely likely that we shall ever adopt a similar plan in this country.
MADGE.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY JULY 4 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JULY 4 1902
LALL Kull:us KESERVEDd
WILMA. MAY,
BARRY PAIN.
PART 1.-CHAPTER I.

Philip Amory was only twenty years old when he decided- to leave England. He had no relations to consult, and his guardian never opposed him in i anything, but his friends—of which n spite of his eccentricities he had many—were indignant. He was leaving Cambridge in the middle of his career there, and the ,career had promised to be very brilliant. He was going to Queensland, and/ Queensland is a long way off. I told him that if he went there he might just as well die, and on the whole I should prefer the death. What made it more irritating was, that he never gave one solid reason for going to Queensland, or even for leav- ing England at all. A man's friends can hardly allow him to make a fool of himself without pro- viding themselves with some plausible explanation, and accordingly we said that there was a woman in the case. It was not a very satisfactory ex- planation, because, if there was a woman in the case, we certainly did not know who the woman Na as. At first he wrote to me frequently. At the end of six months I got one long letter from him, of which the first half was all about horse-breaking, to which he seemed to have given much attention, while the remainder of the letter was occupied with a proposal for a new reading in a passage in one of the "Agamemnon " choruses. To .this letter there was a postscript, "I have married." He did not say whom he had married, or give any other information. I wrote to enquire and to con- gratulate, and sent him silver candlesticks. He never answered that letter or acknowledged the present. I had no further news of him until a little more than a year afterwards, when I hap- pened to see in a paper the announcement of the death of his wife. I wrote to express my sympathy, and he never answered that letter either. I made allowances for his 'erratic nature, but my patience was considerably tried. Years went by, and then one day I got a short note from him :

- - "Dear Edward,—You never told me what you thought of that reading in the ft Agamemnon " which I proposed to you I wish you would. Do you happen to want to buy—or to knon anybody who wants to buy—a quantity of precious opals! Try to answer this at once.
" Yours ever, "Pamir Antony.'

To this I replied : "Dear Phil,—Since you first wrote on the "Agamemnon,' I have forgotten my Greek, but without acquiring in its place any desire to buy opals, or any knowledge of anyone with that desire. You have treated me abominably, and eccentricity does not excuse you. Come back to England, and I will for. give you—but correspondence with you is hopeless. "Yours ever, "EDWARD DERRIMER." One more year passed, and then one morning a 'OW was brought me with the postmark of little Buckinghamsliiro ran:—

- • "Dear Edward,—You declined—rightly, I think—to corres pond with me. My faults as a correspondent are due to several causes. I write letters which I afterwards forget to post. Ido not send news of myself, because it is impossible for me to realise that people must be told things about me which Ido not require to be told about myself. Also, I have been , very busy. However, you said that if I returned to England you would forgive me, and I have returned. I am thirty•two years old, and I have done my roaming. I shall not leave England again. "I have bought Sinden, and settled here with Wilmay. Yon remember that I once told you at Cambridge that I knew of a little spot which I meant to buy one day. That was Sinden—an Elizabethan house and about forty acres of free. hold. The garden is a dream. Wilmay and I want you to come down to-morrow and stay for any period not less than one lunar month. For the sake of old times come, and bring my absolution with you. "Yours ever, "PHILIP AMORY."

"P.S.—Wilmay is the child. Now, that; -Weise in point. How was I to realise that you require to be told that, when I never require to be told it myself?' I hesitated, but the appeal to old times decided me. I wrote him a long letter, abused him for all his little failings, and said that I would most cer, tainly come on the morrow, and my train would arrive at seven in the evening.

As I stood on the platform, watching the reced- ing train that I had just missed, I suppose that I felt and spoke like an angry man, tor the porter mildly suggested that it was not his fault, and that he did not make the trains. "How long is it to the next? Half an hour ? " "Full an hour." I thought of putting off my visit until the morrow rather than dislocate my host's dinner-hour. But my bag was packed, and it did not seem worth while to go back after I had once started. To fill in the time I strolled out into the street, found a telegraph office, and sent off ninepence-halfpenny- worth of my best apologies to Philip. Then it occurred to me that I might buy a present for Wilmay. It was characteristic that even now Philip had never mentioned whether Wilmay was a boy or a girl, but at ten years old the sexes have much in common. I passed a shop where they sold French chocolates, and bought enough to account satisfactorily for my existence to Wilmay —boy or girl. Children mostly like you to produce some such evidence that your life is not quite pur- poseless. I found Philip waiting for me on the station platform at Sin&n. It was twelve years since we had met, and our conversation at first was, while his servant was looking after my luggage, inco- herent—a volley of mixed questions and answers. His dog-cart was waiting outside the station, but Sinden was within five minutes' distance, and at my suggestion we walked. Philip was wonderfully little changed by twelve years as far as personal appearance went. He had looked, perhaps, older than his.years at twenty; at thirty-two he looked younger than he was. Ye was a handsome man— tall, dark, clean-shavea, with the build of an athlete. He occasionally made little gestures while he talked—a habit, by the way, NA Inch lie had never had while we were at Cambridge. "Well," I said, as We walked, "you don't look old enough to be the father IA a child of ten." " Yes,' he said, "Wilmay is ten." "And is Wilmay a boy or a girl?" "A girl, of course. Upon my soul, you don't know the simplest things.' I made the obvious, retort, and he tried further to explain his erratic and abominable conduct. "I know I should have written more often and told you about myself. But then some of your letters absolutely demanded an answer, and that sort I never can answer, and I wasn't always interesting enough to write about. Oh I look here, you shall ask me anything you like at dinner. I will make up all arrears of information then. By the way, 410 you like children?" "You remind me of a girl who once asked me if I like poetry. 'There are children and children." "Well, yes: Wilmay is the other kind." A short avenue of limes brought us up to the front door. My luggage had already arrived, and had been taken up to my room. The man who un- packed it took out four largish boxes of chocolate, and placed them with solemnity in a regular line on the table. You get a good deal of chocolate for a pound or so. I selected a box which was covered with purple satin, and had a heart in gold on the top. "Do you know if Miss Wilmay has gone to bed?" I asked. "I believe not, sir. I will inquire for you.' He brought back word that she had not yet gone to 'bed. "Then would you have this box taken to her, from Mr. Derrimer, with his love ? " That was the introductory or ingratiating offer. ing. I reserved two boxes with which to revivify my popularity from time to time, and one as a farewell offering. The man brought back word that Miss Wilmay desired to thank me very much for the present and the message.

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.

Philip Amory and I were alone at dinner. He talked delightfully, told stories by The dozen, described bush life and mining life, told me a heap of those little interesting things that, travellers forget to put in their books, but told me nothing at all about himself. I thought, perhaps, that he was waiting until the servants had gone. But even then he told me very little, and I hardly liked to accept his invitation to question him. I knew that he had married, and that his wife had died a little more than a year afterwards, shortly after Wilmay's birth. It was quite possible that even after a lapse of. ten years he might feel himself unable to speak of that time. Yowever, he did refer to it once, as we sat smoking in the library. -

"Why don't you get married 11" he asked me. "That is what Bertha is always saying to me." Bertha was my Worldly sister, Mrs. Enterland, at that time thoroughly enjoying her second year of widowhood. "I can only tell you what I always tell Bertha—that, so far, I have never had the opportunity. "You have no resolve against it? 1' "Those that resolve against it, incontinently marry the. housemaid and drop out. No. I've no

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: reserve. But ram thirty-two, spa t nave escapea so far, and I hope—humbly and sdith bated breath—. I hope." , So far we had both spoken flippantly enough. But now he said, quite seriously, looking away from me "You are quite right; never marry. A ,man who marries, in the way that young men marry, risks loss. It becomes his greatest sorrow to remember his greatest' happiness. He wants to Curse God, and die, and perhaps there are reasons why he cannot die. Never marry, never love." There was a long pause. I did not know what to say. , " While I am speaking of this," he rk.3umed, "I want to £,ay that you sent me two letters, for which I have never thanked you, old man. But I was grateful for those letters, and I should like—" "It is not necessary. It's all right I under- stand perfectly." "Then we will not speak of this again. If a man means to go on, and I. mean to go on for another thirty or forty years, and the insurance people seem to think there's a chance of it—if, I say, a man means to go on, he must, by the time he has passed thirty, have got some sort of con- trol over his own thoughts. He must be able to say to himself, Such-and-such an episode is closed; you must not think of this; you must not remember that.'" "Can any man control his own thoughts?" "it is a popular fallacy that he cannot. I do, and many men do. I believe that most men of my age with the average history—or a history ever so little worse than the average—must either learn to do that, or must go mad. But enough—we will talk of other things." Perhaps it was because I had not his facility for putting things out of my mind. Certainly, although we did talk of other things, for some time we spoke with some seriousness and constraint. Gradually we got back to the old manner. " Do you remember," he said, "that I wrote to you about some opals? You took that solemnly— at the foot of the letter. It was only my way of conveying to you the news that I was dealing in 'opals. I had fifteen hundred pounds' worth of them lying on the big table at which I sat when I wrote to you. But I didn't mean that I wanted you to find me a market for them." "When you write to a man who is in a bad temper, underline anything which is not to be taken seriously, and tell him you've done it, then he may possibly understand you. However, you did well with your opals, if Sinden is the result." "Not as well as I should have done. Opals do not fetch their real value yet—they will, but at present they don't. I tried other things, too, but we needn't go into the details of money-grubbing. Not being a Crcesus like yourself, I had to grub and did grub. It would have been too absurd for Wilmay not to have had anything she wanted. However, it's over now." It is, perhaps, as well that I should explain that I was not a Crcesus. I had an annual income of ELMO a year, and no prospect that it would ever be increased. Indeed, as it was derived in part from the rent of agricultural land, it promised to grow less. I asked him how long he had been at Sinden. "I have been here," he answered, "one week to-day. I have only behn in England a fortnight. I had an agent here watching for a chance to buy Sinden for me, and as soon as he cabled to me that he had got it I returned." I was rather surprised. There was nothing in the furniture or arrangements of the house which indicated so recent an occupation. There was nothing temporary or makeshift. I said as much, and he explained that he had been lucky in mak- ing people do things for him the way he wanted them done. He said that on the next day he and Wilmay would show me the ,place. "Tell me about Wilmay,' I said. she like ? " He turned his head, smiled, and told me to see for myself. I looked round. I had not heard a sound, but the library door had been opened and Wilmay stood there. After all these years I have but to close my eyes, and I can still see Wilmay as I saw her then—a white figure standing in the dark ',doorway. She was in a long white nightgown. Her feet were bare exquisitely shaped, looking as if they were made of rose-petals. Her hair, of the palest gold, hung down below her waist. Her deep blue child's eyes were fixed on her father and myself. In one hand she carried the box of chocolates, the other hand was stretched out as she came forward. She had the face of an angel. " Wilmay," said her father, Mr. Edward Derrimer." She shook hands with me without the least shy- ness. "Your Uncle Edward," I said, "if I may have that honour, a sort of supernumerary, un- official uncle." "I would sooner call you just Edward, if I may., I don't like the word uncle,' or the word 'meals,' or ulcer,' oh, and there are some other words too 1 The sound of them is so bad." "By all means call me Edward. And what am I to call you—Will ?" "Never I" she laughed. "Nobody calls me that. Only Wilmay." She made herself comfortable in is low lounge chair, and opened the purple box. "It's so hot to-night, and I couldn't sleep. So I thought I would come downstairs just as I was, and try to find you. I did send a message, but I wanted to thank you myself for this lovely box and the chocolates. How did you know that I liked chocolates ?" "It was a wild guess of mine." "It was quite right. See I've eaten half a row already. If," she added, pensively, "I were tO eat four more, I should be ill." I looked for, some proper and conventional display of paternal authority. None came. Her father sat and watched her and me with an amused smile. I, therefore, took it upon myself to suggest that the box should be closed until the morrow. I did not want to have the death of the child on my conscience. "Oh, no 1" she said. "As four would perhaps make me ill, I skan't eat four. I shall eat three." And she did. Then she said that her father had told her that I was a fine musician. I suggested some slightly milder term as being more likely to Come within a hundred miles of the truth. Philip would have called any man a musician who was capable of playing a Beethoven sonata with any approach to correctness and feeling. It was generous of him, but misleading. But Wilmay was not to be denied. She said that eh. wanted me to make some music for her. Philip rose apparently taking it for granted that I should what the child wanted. "We must come into the nest room, then," he said. "There's a piano there." It was a good instrument. "It was tuned yesterday," said Wilmay, "by a man who smelt of sherry and told me to trot along. 'Trot along '.has a bad sound, too." I sat down to the piano, and did not in the least know what to play. It occurred to me that nursery rhymes might possibly appeal, and I tried some of them. When I had finished Wilmay came up to the piano and said, "Do you know this?" She hummed a scrap of the Tannhauser March. She hummed in tune. "Yes," I said. " Would you please play it ? " "Well." I said, "on a piano you can't—abut no matter, I'll do my best." If she had asked me to give her some idea of a Mendelssohn organ sonata on a penny whistle, Philip would have expected me to comply without a murmur. When I had finished she put both arms round my neck, kissed me impulsively, said "good night,' and ran out of the room. "'Well," said Philip, when she had gone. "Yes," I said, "Wilmay is the other kind." "By the way," I added, when we had gone back to the library and lit our cigars, "I am not a father, and I have no experience of children. At the same time, it I let things pass without com- ment, I may be made an accessory after the fact, or something equally unpleasant. Do you allow a child of ten to get out of bed and catch her death of cold by wandering about the house with only her night-gown on? Do you allow her to execute that wandering barefooted, when she may tread on a tin-tack, get blood poisoning, and die of it Do you allow her to ruin her health by sitting up until long after eleven, or to shatter what seems at present a quite useful digestion by unrestricted apd excessive indulgence in chocolates? Forgive these questions—but I have still some rudiments of a conscience." Philip laughed and told me I was an old woman. -in, and she -mid not—and
"What is
"This is Edward—

The night Was very warm, . she wom— knew she could not—catch cold. The floor of the house was not—and she knew it was not—composed of inverted tin-tacks. Also Philip himself regarded it as foolish to stop in bed when you could not sleep. He pointed out that the "excessive indul- gence" was not proved, and that it was I who had put the temptation in her way. "But after all," he said, "I never allow or forbid. In Wilmay's case it is not necessary, and in the case

ot almost ail children it is nothing nice so necessary as is supposed." 1 "What? You have theories of the education of children as well as of horse-breaking." "I have pretty much the same theory in both cases—the least possible interference with the ordinary development of nature. I have studied wild men and wild horses. I have found in both something valuable that the common method of education and civilisation kills." "From what I've read of primitive people, I should say that generally they were chiefly remark- able for dirtiness, ignorance, and brutality." "Well, if you yourself lived among the Esqui- maux, or if you were at the mines in a time of bad drought, you would not wash. The struggle for life brings out as much brutality here as you'll find among the Apaches, but in different forms. But don't misunderstand me—l did not say no interfe- rence with nature at all. I said the least possible. In the case of the horse, the least possible means quite a good deal, though less than is generally supposed. In the case of the child in general, the least possible interference means but little interfe- rence." "But that question of ignorance—children are ignorant, and they don't want to learn. They have to be made to learn." " I answer you in your own words—there are children and children. I'm not trying to push my point to an extreme. I have no illusions about it. There are many children—boys especially—who won't learn anything if they can help it. But it's our own fault because we begin by ordering them about and saying, Obey me and learn this, when if we could shew them that the particular knows ledge was to their pleasure and sdvantage, Nature herself would urge them to acquire it." "I know you've broken horses. Have you edu- cated children? or is this merely your habit of theorising ? " "I have more or less educated Wilmay. She could ride long before she could read. She did not begin to learn to read until two years ago. I used to read Hans Andersen to her. _ One day it struck her that if she knew how to read, she would be able to read Hans Andersen when I was not there. So she wanted to learn—and did learn with unusual rapidity. Six months ago she decided that she would learn to write." "Do you do the actual teaching ? " "No. -Wilmay's woman, Mrs. Blayd, does that: I don't teach—l only stop other people from teach- ing until the right time comes. There are no regular lesson hours for Wilmay—she begins work when she likes and stops when she likes." "In fact, she does everything she likes—has never learned self-control, or methodical habits, or regard for the feeling of others, and has been absolutely spoiled by a father who sits up of nights inventing theories to cover his own laziness, weakness, and eccentricity." He laughed cheerfully. "Wait and see," he said. " Wilrnay's not faultless, but before you have been here a month you will own that my system is the right system—for her at any rate." I never did make this humiliating confession to him. When some weeks later he asked me for it, I contented myself with saying that Will-nay was apparently a child who could not be spoiled, even by a father with a mass of mad theories. •

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.

We sat very late that night talking, and when we separated we mutually agreed that ten o'clock or thereabouts would be the right hour for break- fast. However, I woke at six, went to sleep, and woke again once every ten minutes until shortly after seven, and then rang my bell and got up. When I was dressed I went downstairs and out into the garden. I found Wilmay there, and she came up to look after me. She shook hands, and asked me if I wouldn't like to have breakfast at once. "No, thanks," I said, "the excellent Carter has, just asked me the same question. But I've had some tea, and I'd rather wait until your father comes down. Have you had breakfast ? ' "Not yet; I thought I would have breakfast with you two this morning." I said that would be charming. She took me off to see the garden and the stables. On the way it occurred to her that it weuld be pleasant to have breakfast on the lawn. ' "We do, sometimes, when it's a good morning like this." I thought the idea capital. She called up an under-gardener, and said with much dignity : " Would you kindly go up to the house, and let Carter know that we should like breakfast on the lawn this morning?" It was very quaint—l was amused. While she was showing me her own pony she suddenly asked if I considered that music was as difficult to learn as writing. I said that it was more difficult, more heart- breakint. I ought really, in self-defence' to have put it much stronger than this. I had guessed what would happen. I had made her want to learn music, and she would learn it, and—this was the horror of it—l was to give her her first lessons. I had always been in the habit of saying that I believed there must be a special reward hereafter for music-masters, because in this life they have to suffer more than other men. It was at breakfast time that the moment arrived when I felt that I had either to consider myself a brute or to offer to teach Wilmay the piano. I Eet my teeth; and made the offer. She thanked me, and said that it would be lovely, but that she must not bother me and take up my time. That, of course, finished it. By the end of break- fast I was imploring as a privilege to be allowed to teach Wilmay the piano, and Wilmay was sweetly and graciously consenting. I told Philip after- wards that I thought in common decency he ought to have protested, and said firmly that he would not allow any guest of his to be turned into a music-master in his house. He smiled and said that he could not see it. "Very well," then," I answered. "I will have regular hours for those lessons, and keep to them, and break up your go-as-you-please system." At this he only smiled again. Wilmay and I decided upon regular hours, and sometimes we kept to them. I may, perhaps, have torgotten about them three or four times—not, more. As I pc'nted out to Philip, it was better than not even attempting to be regular. Wilmay was an excellent pupil. She learned quickly, but then she worked of her own accord far harder than most children would have worked under compulsion. I do not pretend that these lessons • were an unmixed joy to me. I doubt if elementary lessons on the piano to a child of ten are ever an unmixed joy to anybody. But I had expected that they would be very much worse. Wilmay really loved music. As a reason for my existence, music seemed to do even better than chocolates, though probably those four boxes helped to solve the problem. I chaffed Philip occasionally about his system of educating a child by leaving out the education and allowing her to do as she liked. But, speaking seriously, that system had answered admirably with Wilmay. It seemed to have given het a spirit, an independence, a readiness of initiative, that one very rarely finds in children of that age. She knew what to do. And, I confess it, she was not spoiled. She seemed to have an innate sweet- ness, tenderness, and unselfishness of nature that was proof against spoiling. She gave orders to the servants just as, Philip woald have done, and the servants were, apparently, instructed to take her. orders as his own, but I never knew her give a dic- tatorial or unreasonable order, or omit to thank a servant who had done anything for her. Her own woman, Mrs. Blayd, was devoted to her. Mrs. Blayd was a blend of nurse, governess, and lady's maid, and also rather gave one the impression that she was a lady herself. She was a middle-aged woman, very quiet and reserved. Philip told me that she had been with Wilmay ever since her birth. •

During the next three years I saw Philip and Wilmay very frequently. Sometimes I went down to Ayshurst. Once or twice my married sister, Mrs. Enterland, had Philip and Wilmay to stay with her at her house in Mayfair. Bertha is a worldly little woman, with few ideals, and those mostly wrong, but before she began to be worldly she hail a kind heart, and there are still traces of it left. I had talked to her about Philip arid Wilmay, and she was eager to know them. I put it off as long as I could, because Bertha is the very opposite of Philip, and I thought the meeting would be a failure. But Bertha insisted, and the meeting was not a failure. It was a toss-up whether Bertha would decide that Philip was " U.,ioniat" or " very interesting." Philip was good-looking man, and he dressed well when ha was in London, and he saved her from beini swindled over some carriage horses, and he spent money extravagantly, and he had a history which he did not tell her Or anybody else. These things taken together made him in her eyes very inter- esting. Of course, there never was any doubt at all about Wilmay. She charmed everybody, and never knew it. It was when Wilmay was just fourteen that I had asked her and Philip to co_me and stop with

me at a Little cottage that / had on tne river. There was no river at Ayshurst, and both of them were fond of boating. On the morning of the day when they should have arrived I received a telegram from Philip "Come to Sinden at once. Most urgent.'3 (To be continued.)
TO DIE WITH HER HUSBAND.

div.head: Woman's Pathetic Wish.
div.p: Woman's Pathetic Wish.

IVING at a typical farm- house, "Old Mumford," Kingsnorth, Ashford. Mrs Sarah Cook, the wife of a shepherd. Wiiliam Cook,is heroine of a pathetic story in the annals of that rustic community. Mrs Cook, a native of Somerset- shire, came to live in Kent some sixteen years ago. She soon tecame se ill with indigestion that a doctor was called in but the ailment re.

Mac S. Coos. mined chronic and in. (From a photograph by A. B. curable by all ordinary Da'Ath, Tunbridge Wells.) medicine, and it was thought she would not recover, until Dr Wil:iams' pink pills for pale people were tried. There bad first, however, been a sudden acute attack. and ehe had been told t y a doctor in her native county whore she went for a change, that she had better go home at onco, as she WANTED TO DIE WITH HER HUSBAND.

The following are her own words : " About five years ago, the indigestion often came on so severely that I used to roll about the floor in agony. I was doubled op with pain. When I went upstairs I had to go a few steps at a time and rest between. I locked so bad that all the neighbours spoke about it. "I felt my life was not worth living," oontinued Mrs Cook, "but I said to my husband, ' I will try Dr Williams' pink pills,and if they don't do me any good I must die.' He got me some and I found benefit before I had taken quite a box. I could begin to eat, and the pains gradually passed away. After a second box I could eat anything. That was three years ago and I have been going on well ever since. I have had no return of dyspepsia nor the wind spasms whieh I used to have round the heart. "These pills have cured me, and I cannot speak too highly of them. See what they have done for me. For three years I never shook a bed, but now I can do any- thing ; I could net walk round the table without holding to it for support, whereas I now think nothing of walk- ing to Ashford and back—over five miles. Yes, lam a different woman." _ . . .

Lack of power to digest and extract nourishment from food is the state of thousands, and the result is seen in haggard men and women embittered by per- petual gnawing pain. Tbe stomach requires "tone." or strength and the strength necessary is supplied by Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people,which enrich the blood in an unequalled manner. div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
LANCASHIRE v. YORKSHIRE.

The eighth annual meeting bet wean representative teams of the two counties was opened on Saturday over the green of the Friday Club of Old Trafford. The attendance was less numerous that usual. The earlier wins went much in favour of the home side, but the visitors recovered themselves just before half time, and at one period were seven points to the fore. Later play not only restored the lead to Lancashire, but enabled them to secure a win by 44 shots, a larger majority than they have obtained since the summer of 1899. Crowther Hirst, the Huddersfield trundler, who holds the distinc- tion of having the Yorkshire Individual Merit on two occasions, and is this year's champion, met defeat, his conqueror being H Williams (Warrington) who stole a march on him to the extent of five points. div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
Warrington Again Defeated.

Warrington met Hyde Seal at Hyde Corporation Bathe, on Tuesday evening, the match being in connection with the North of England Champion- ship. Both clubs were strongly represented. he game opened fast, Warrington being first to score. Immediately afterwards Hyde equalized by Dobson. and Tom Hodson improved Hyde's total. At tde interval Hyde led by two goals to one. Hyde started well in the second half, but the forwards were very weak in shooting. Eventually, from a beautiful pass by Dobson, Hodson scored a third goal, and shortly afterwards the same player added I a fourth. Result; Hyde Seal, four goals; Warring- ton, one.

Tired with the exertions of pleasure 'seeking they returned home at various hours, the last train reaching Warrington shortly after midnight. THE RICHMOND GAS-STOVE AND METER COMPANY, LIMITED. Blackpool was the venue of this well-known tirm's excursion, andithe employee will long retain pleasant recollections of the outing. Excellent arrangements had been made to ensure the success of the trip, and praise is due to Mr. T. F. Davy, upon whom most of this work devolved. A special train left Bank Qatty Station at six o'clock, the passengers numbering over seven hundred. Saloons were provided for the foremen of departments and their wives and friends. After a pleasant journey the popular resort was reached at about 7 40. and the excursionists dispersed to enjoy themselves as inclination dictated. Through- out the day the sun shone brilliantly from a clear blue sky, and the only drawback to pleasure seek- ing was the oppressive heat. Blackpool presented a bright and festive appearance, the town having been lavishly decorated in anticipation of the Coro- nation. The fine promenade was gay with stream- ers, and a pleasing innovation was the artistic deccration of the tramcars. Extensive preparations for illuminations had been made, and it Was a matter of regret to the visitors that the time of their departure did not enable them to witness the display. Excursions poured into the town from all parts, and the streets were in a crowded state. The Warrington trippers found ample means of occupy- ing their time pleasurably, the Tower, Winter Gardens, and other amusement palaces being freely patronized. Sea-trips and rides on the electric cars were other popular forms of enjoyment. A cycle parade took place in the afternoon and was watched with interest by many. The return journey was commenced at 9.20, Warrington being reached shortly after midnight after a most successful excursion. OTHER TRIPS TO BLACKPOOL. There were several other trips from Warrington to Blackpool. The employees of Mr R A Naylor, Howley Timber Mills, journeys i in a special train which left Bank Quay station at 6.25, reaching Talbor-road at 8.30. At nine o'clock a start was made for War- rington, which was reached at 11.15, all voting the outing to have been a most enjoyable one. Great credit is due to Mr Elenshall, who was responsible for the whole of the day'a arrangements, The workmen of Mossrs Themlis and Griffit'ThMersey- street, also went to Blackpool, the firm ireaerously pay- ing the railway expenses ef attout 130 employes, who were accompanied by their wives arid friends. The train left Bank Quay Station at 6.30, and returned to War- rington at about ten o'clock. The men were accom- panied by Messrs Davies and Lingard, the managers. About 150 of the employes of the Castle Rubber Com- pany and friends also spent the day at the earns place in an equally enjoyable manner. The men made their own arrangements, and were free to go where they wished on their arrival at Tsibot-road Sta ion. div.head: NOTES ON LAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON LAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Considering the weak team which did duty for War- rington on Saturday, it was hardly to be expected that the encounter at Bolton would end in victory. for the visiting eleven. As it was, the Warringtonians were thoroughly beaten, this being the second reverse they have sustained this season. The team lacked the ser- vices of such useful players as kessrs Bibby, Gibbon, Callon, and , Silcock, whilst Lynes had sustained an injury to the hand which rendered it practically impossible for him to bat. The Bolton contingent went to the wicket first, and had compiled the highly creditable total of 154- for the loss of three wickets when the closure was applied. The Warringtonians made a feeble response, all the players being dismissed for 95.

Ellis, the well-known Bolton professional, did some excellent work with the willow, his innings being pro- ductive of no fewer than 73 runs. Creditable totals were also attained by Vost (241,1 Stanley (17), and Thnperlake (161,the two last-named players not having been got out when the innings closed.

The brothers Connor made a capital stand for the Warringtonians, E A Connor being responsible for 31 and E Connor for 23. The only other batsman to attain double _figures was Bishop, who contributed 15.

The second eleven also suffered defeat, the Bolton second being victorious by 44 runs. Additional interest was lent to the engagement by the appearance in the home ranks of two new players who have gained dig- Unction in the football world—F Barber and J Hallam. The last-named player batted splendidly, running up a total of 37. Barber fared badly, his innings realizing only one run. Unsworth (14) and Richardson (11) gave valuable assistance to the Warring,tonians. For Bolton, the top scorers were E Feather (21.), NV Cunliffe (16), S Greenhalgh (30 not out), Hawkins (19), and E Redford (16). Several Warrington bowlers acquitted themselves well, D Plinston taking five wickets for 48 runs. Bennett two for 30, C H Unsworth two for 14, and C R, Adamson one for four.

we paid the money. Everyone would prefer money to an agreement. The money was paid sufficiently long ago for the work to be completed by now. With refer- ence to the paving of streets after the tramways had been laid be hoped the commictee would accelerate the work. The tramways had been running tor some menthe and half the work of paving still remained to be done. Councillor Ems°le said he attended a place of wor- ship which the care passed, and he had a ()elm hint to make with reference to the sounding of (be gongs. The DEPUTY MAYOR in reply said the drivers had had instructions not to sound the gong when passing places of worship except under exceptional circumstances, and generally hie, thought they carried out their instructions. With reference to Councillor Tinnion's complaint about himself (Alderman Roberts), it was rather depressing when a mile who was conscious of his physical infirm- ity, and who had been trying for a considerable period to cultivate a spirit of meekness—(laughter)—found there was no recognition of it in quarters where one ex- pected to end that recognition. (Renewed laughter.) He had been under the impression that he was suppress- ing the old enemy to an extent which did him a con- siderable amount of credit. (Laughter.) The click. clicking which was Said to be very objectionable was not the only click-clacking which was going on in Warrinvon and which was equally objectionable,if not more so. But everything should be done that was possible to minimize the nsise. ati had intended to refer to the Wilderapool delay, when he moved the adoption of the report, but he overlooked the mat,er. If there wee a member of the Council who made a conspicuous failure when he attempted to be sarcestic, it was their friend Alderman Bolton. (Laughter.) The fac's from the Corporation point of view were simply these. Oa the 22nd March the estimated arneuet which the Railway Company's engineer certified would be required for the alteration of the permanent way was paid. On the 19th April they paid a further cheeps for the estimated amount certi- fied by the company's engineer for providing the inter- locking signals required, and so far as the committee were conoerned they had carried out their work. Why on earth the Landon and North-Western Railway Com- pany lad not preceeied with the work earlier passed his wisdom and knowledge to explain. He quite agreed that the delay was most discreditable,and was imposing ' serious disabilities on the town. They had put the , matter before the csineany again in strong terms this week, and he hoped the protestation would show that while the company as a big corporation were extremely slew to move the Corporation et Warrington were trying to meet all reasonable requirements themselves. The Corporation felt that they were not being fairly and reasonably de sit with in regard to the time which ' was being taken by the railway company in thus matter. The Corporation had not shown the Railway Company the same spirit of aoathy in mitten where they were concerned as the reilwee c mapany had shown in this. The agreement had nothing to do w ith the alteration to the permanent way, or with the jut erlocking signals but with the manipulation of the traffic over the line after the work was completed, There had been no delay OR the part of the Corp 'radon, which bad resulted from the fact that the agreement Lied not been signed earlier than the date to which Alderman Rotten had referred. The company tried to impose ce rtaia conditions of an onerous character, which the Corporation engineers refused to agree to. La the meantime the company had both the cheques of the Corporation, and they might have proceeded with the execution of the work for which they had been paid in advance. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then agreed to.

div.head: TRAMWAYS,
div.p: THE TRAMWAYS,
The Position of Stockton Heath.
Delay in the Opening of the Nilderspool Route. Protest Against the Railwai Company's Dilatoriness.

"Click-Clacking." several matters of importance affecting the tramway system in Warrington were under discus- sion at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The minutes of the Tramways Committee stated that the Town Clerk reported that the Board of Trade had sanctioned the borrowing of the further sum of £27,000 for tramway purposes. The following letter from the Borough Surveyor was read :—" Town Hall, Warrington, June 4th 1902. The Chairman and members of the Tram- ways Committee. Gentlemen,—ln accordance with the resolution of your committee :—' That the Borough Surveyor report at the next meeting on the cost of making Winwick-road suitable for train rails whore the water mains have b3en laid,' the Borough Surveyor begs to report that he has examined the foundation of the road and finds that where the single tram lines are proposed to be laid the specified thickness of concrete will be sufficient. Where double lines or cross-overs are proposed the line is ever the water trench, which in length is about 450 yards, and it is essential that 12in. of concrete should be laid to support the tram rails. This work will entail an extra expenditure of about £35.-1 remain gentlemen,yours obediently,Tnoeus LONODIR, Borough Engineer and Surveyor." It was resolved that the above recommendation be agreed to. It was resolved that the Town Clerk report at the next meeting on the Warrington Light Railway Order, and that Messrs Preece and Cardew be asked to furnish an estimate of the cost of carrying out railway No 1 on the conditions m posed by the Order. It was agreed to issue weekly tickets at Is each to school children using, the tram care, such tickets not to be available for Saturdays and Sundays. Tenders for four addi- tional tram cars were opened, and sent to Messrs Preece and Cardew for report. It was decided that an application be made to the Board of Trade for an extension of time for the completion of the tramways. A petition was read from the reli- dents in and about Padgate-lane requesting the committee to construct Tramway No 7 ; and it was resolved that the consideration of the petition be deferred until the committee have had an oppor- tunity of inspecting the route. The Town Clerk reported that the Board of Trade had sanctioned the borrowing of the further sum of £27,000 for tramway purposes.—The question of repaving with wood in front of places of worship was considered, and it was decided that the cost could not be borne by the committee. STATEMENT BY THE CHAIRNIAN OF THE TRAMWAYS COMMITTEE. The DEPUTY-MAYOR, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the borrowing of the further sum of £27,000 for tramway purposes. He explained that it formed part of the original estim- ate and was required for the Manchester-road and Winwick-road sections. With regard to Railway No. 1, he seriously feared that the conditions which had been imposed on the committee by the Light Railway Commissioners,at the request of the people of Stockton Heath, were such as might possibly prevent the construction of the light railway. At any rate the position of the committee was simply this : they had as business men to consider this extraordinary outlay, with the conditions attached, which practically nearly doubled it. The !same length of line under ordinary conditions in War- rington would cost little more than half what this light railway would cost, and for which they would not receive a single additional peony in income so far as they could see, By the order which had been made the Corporation could not charge any more for conveying passengers to Victoria-square than they could for conveying them to the present ter- minus at Stafford-road. Taking all these matters into considered ea be could not help saying that he thought the very good people of Stockton Heath had been extremely ill-advised in seeking to impose conditions upon the committee which would cost such an additional amount of money. If the com- mittee could not see that they could make money out of the scheme they would let it drop, and if so the people of Stockton Heath had only themselves to theme, The application to the Board of Trade for an extension of time for the completion of the tearaways was only a formal matter, and the cost would be nominal. With reference to the petition from Padget°, before they came to any de- cision about the matter the committee would visit the locality. Then there was the question of re- paving with wood in front of places of worship. The committee died not think the trams added any- thing to the discomfort of people worshipping in any church or chapel by the traffic taken over the lines. The traffic was comparatively silent. Councillor TINNION I beg your pardon. (Laughter.) The DEPUTY MAYOR: I said comparatively Silent. Ahlerman Slum' GREEN: I should like you to define that. The DEPUTY MAYoit replied that the traffic which made the:noise was the traffic which went, over the setts. Comparatively speaking the traffic over the metals was silent, compared with that which went over the setts. If the Paving and Sewerage Committee thought it desirable to take up the wlride of the sett pavement in front of places of Worship, the Tramways Committee was pre- pared to do the portion within the tram-lines and a few inches on each side. Alderman MoNxs seconded. Councillor TINNION alluded to the resolution " that the Paving and Sewerage Committee be recommended to make arrangements with the contractors for the re-paving, according to schedule of prices, of all streets intertered with by tram- ways," This matter of the interference of the stceets by the Tramways Committee, was of vast importance, and would b 3 an eye opener to the ratepayers when the bill came to be paid. He had never understood why it was ;necessary to alter the levels in so many places. However, the Paving and Sewerage Committee were having a special meeting next week to consider the matter, when the question of the Whole of the levels of the streets would be gone into. Whether it was pos- sible to avoid such extensive alteration Of the streets was a matter which could not be decided at present. It was a question that was very pressing. Accidents had been reported and claims Made only this week in reference to the condition of tbe roads caused by the alterations for the tramways. With reference to the re-paving with wobd in front of places of warship the committee found that the cost would be enormous. The whole of the re-pav- ing would cost from £lO,OOO to £14,000. The Deputy Mayor said somewhat heatedly-- The DEPUTY MAYOR: I am never more surprised in my life. (Laughter.) Councillor TINNION, continuing, said the Aldermen had remarked somewhat heatedly for an ordinary mem- ber of the Council—(laughter)—that the noise of the trams was comparatively silent. In his (Councillor Tinnion's) town house in Winmarieigh-street, at the corner, be bad the benefit of the clacking arrangement, I but if the track was watered it would be a great bsuefit, land there would be less friction and waste of power. The noise was more like an out-of-joint and worn-out steam roller than a tramway —(laughter)—and one could laardlylhear an ordinary conversation in a house. Be had beard complaints about the noiereof the trams going round the Corners and the click-clacking. They had also the benefit of the bell. If he could judge a the noise made and the large amount of traffic on Sundays be should be very much surprised if congregations in places of worship were not much disturbed. Councillor BENNETT. referring to the Padgatr-lane petition, suggested a circular route through King Edward-street, Zse. That would probably be the most serviceable route, and as the committee were about to inspect the place be hoped they wculd favourably con- sider the request of the petitioners. The petition had been very influentially signed, and be hoped the corn- mittee would favourably consider the request of the petitioners. He would like some explination of the cause of the delay in the opening of the Wilderspool route. He was told there were difficulties with the Landon and North-Western Railway Company. They had a groat respect for a railway company, but it was monstrous that such a company should be allowed week after week to stand in the way of the legitimate require- ments of an important town like Warrington. He hoped the committee were using all the exertion they could in the matter to bring the railway company—he was going to use a stronger term,and say bring them to their senses —to accelerate the process by which a railway company brought itself into harmony with the requirements of a town. (Hear, hear). Alderman BOLTON said he was surprised to find that the work was so very backward, but the contract was not signed until the 18th June' and six months would elapse before the work would be done. (Laughter.) The agreement with the railway company ought to have been signed at an earlier date. Alderman MONKS : Instead of signing the agreement

" Ah, my dear Miss Marie," he said, with beautiful courtesy, "one so bright as you does not need to pause in order to reflect." He got her, of course. MAGISTRATE (t 0 defendant) : "You are accused of having terribly beaten two night-watchmen last night. What tempted you to do this?" De- fendant "My feeling of humanity, your worship, because for one night-watchman that beating would have been too much." " YOU'VE my seat, sir," said a man in a train, who had left his seat for a moment. "There is nothing to show that you have retained this seat." • "Look up there. That is my hat box on the rack over this seat." "Well, air, you sit up there on the rack if you have retained a seat up there." Jun So.—Mrs. Hoon : "Why are people who get married often called the contracting par- ties ?' " Mr. Hoon :"I don't know about the bride, but think how small the groom usually looks !" " WIIA.T is the matter ? " asked a lawyer of his coachman. "The horses are running away, sir." "Can't you pull them up?" "I'm afraid not." "Then," said the lawyer, after meditating a moment, "run them into something cheap." HE: "Darling, am I the first man yoiy-ever were engaged to?" She (indignantly): "figir I Do you think that I could live for 26 years where there were other men about without having a chance till you came along?" MRS. PECK.: "You are a queer man. At dinner yesterday, when the Joneses and the Jenkinses were here, I had to do all the talking. You had absolutely nothing to say." Mr. Peck: "You are mistaken. I had plenty teeny, but I never got a. chance to say it." MASTER—" What do you mean by using such language? Are you master here, or amI?" C;erk—" I'm not the master, -of course, but—" Master—" Then why do you talk like an

idiot ? " GUEST: "What have yougqot : " Waiter: "I've got liver,on wet: brains, p a desripitiosn feOf; your Guest: peculiarities. What have you got to eat is what I want to know." BIRDS OF A FEATHER.—SeIf-posseased Bather: "Why, my good fellow, you mustn't bite me." . Hungry Shark: "Why not ? " Self possessed Bather: "Why, I'm-the proprietor of the Skinnem and Fleecem Grand Hotel, don't cher know; pro- fessional courtesies! Ha! ha 1" FOREMAN of pipe-layers, who has been across the street: "I say, how many lengths of pipes did you lay while I was getting my drop of beer ?" Assistant : "Three, sir—fifteen feet each." Fore- man: "Bother it, then my coat is buried just forty-five feet up the street. I left it tucked in the pipe for safety." But for all that he found it in the one last laid down. "WON'T you give me your new baby brother, Nellie ?" asked a visitor of a little four-year-old miss. "No, indeed!" replied Willie, ' I want him to play with. But I'll get you a piece of paper and you can cut a pattern of him. SHE: "There is a great deal of unfairness in this world. Women are barred out of society for things that men may do with impunity." He: "That may be true; but, on the other hand, men would be 'barred out of society if they did some things that women do with impunity every day." She: "I'd like to have you name just one of them." He: "Well, kissing other people's wives and daughters and sweethearts, for instance." A DOMESTIC MYSTERY.—Hubby (walking the floor at 2 a.m.) : "I'd just like to know why this baby persists in staying awake every night?" Wifey : "Really, I can't imagine. I never have any trouble keeping him asleep in the day- time." USUALLY SO.—D: "Honestly, now, what kind of weather do you like best?" E: "That is a subject that has bothered me a great deal. On mature reflection I think the weather that I like best is the weather we are not having at the time." MRS. RUSHER: "Has Mr. Goldcoin, with whom you have been dancing all the evening, at last declared his intentions, Mabel ?" Mabel: "Yes, mother." Mrs. Rusher: "I am so glad! And what did he say?" Mabel: "He declared he would never marry." "GIVE an example of an immovable obstacle," said the teacher; and the smart boy at the foot of the class suggested three girls on the side-walk. The teacher, who usually had to walk in the ' middle of the street herself, sent him right up to the head of the class, and told him to stay there for a week. RATHER STRONG.—" Tobacco smoking," said a traveller, "is so common in Holland, that it is altogether impossible to distinguish one person from another in a room full of smokers." 'But supposing you want to speak to someone present, how are you to find him out?" "Ah ! in such cases a waiter is sent round with a pair of bellows, with which he blows away the smoke from the face of every person until the right one is found." TIME CHANGES.—This is a baby. It is a girl baby. How very bad tempered! How red her -eyes. What horrid contortions she makes with her face. See how savagely she kicks. How like a demon she yells I \Yet in a few short years some man will be half crazy with wild suspense, wor- shipping the very air this being breathes, devoutly kneeling at her feet, and frantically begging for one word, one pressure of the hand, even a look, which will give him hope. The last Friday ii June is always set apart for the great children's festival, and when the news of the King's illness was received the Coronation Committee did not consider it necessary to postpone this portion of the arranged festivities. Favoared with glorious weather, toe event passed off with complete success lest Friday. Forty-two school; took part in the united processios in the morning, and the gaily decorated streets were lined with thousands of spectat ers. The children did not, as on an ordinary Walking Day. assemble on the lawn in front of the Town Hall. They went to various points of rendezvous, and were called upon from these poiutP by the police and formed into a united procession. The Chief Constable ' and his staff began to organise the precession promptly at 9 a.m., and the first school (Wycliffe) entered Bank Park at that hour, The other Nonconformist Retools followed, then culla the Ceureh of Eugland schools, and afterwards the Roman Catholics. Many epeeist features had heed introduced int) the procession for Coronation year, and there was a variety of patriotic emblems. As usual, the Roman C.tbelics bad a brilliant display. There were many beauiful banners, of flue tex- ture and workmanship, depicting the seven Sacraments of the Church, the deceit' of Saints, &.. and a statue of the Blessed Virgin was carried by tour young men. It was placed under a canopy of Artistically arranged tiger fillies and ivy, Cee ainers of flew:ire being carried by the echolars• The children were very prettily attired, those attending St Bone liet'e being dressed in white with brad heliotrope sheshes. They carried in their hands crossos of lilies and arches of flowers with flower streamers added greatly to the beauty of the procession.—Admirable arrangements for the marshell- ing of the procession haci been made ley the Chief Con- stable (Mr Luke Talbotichief marshal), and not a single hitch occurred. The ,marshals were—Mr James G Craik and Mr R T Fairclough, who were assisted by Messrs F G 'Taylor, F Pendlebury, J Eckersl3v, J Draper,R Collin and John Craik. Alter taking port in the procession most of the Noncoaformist scholars left the town for country resorts. whilst the Church at England and Roman Catholic children proceeded So various fi..?lds in town,where sports Szc.,were indulged in. At night a large number of townspeople went to Hill Warren,whara the huge bonfire which bad been prepared for Coronation Day, was lighted by the Idaycress. Some idea ot the magnitude of the fire may he gained when it is stated that it was composed of 140 tone of wood, and five tone of inflammable material such as resin, naphtha, refuse L from the gas works, etc. The whole was thoroughly saturated with about 40 gallons of paraffin ell.
