div.head: KING EDWARD AND QUEEN ALEXANDRA. DRIVING TO
div.p: KING EDWARD AND QUEEN ALEXANDRA. DRIVING TO
BUCKINGHAM PALACE ON MONDAY, JUNE 23RD.
A RECEPTION AS MUST HAVE MADE THEIR HEARTS GLAD.

Words are hardly adequate to express the state of upset and consternation which has reigned through- out England, and especially in London, since the untoward postponement of the Coronation last Tuesday week, and the sudden bathos of the nation from joy to sorrow. This year there has practically been no talk of anything but Coronation, and at length, when everything was prepared, came a postponement, such as could never have been anticipated by the most pessimistic, within forty- eight hours of the ceremony itself. The consequent dislocation of plans and the blow to trade can scarcely be estimated even now, as it seemed impossible for any slip 'twixt the Crown and the King; and of all, perhaps, the newspaper world suffered the greatest loss and inconvenience, many of the weeklies, owing to the holidays, having gone to press and being full of Coronation matter, which seemed out of place. But no one—paper proprietors, seat-holders, seat-vendors, caterers, job-masters, and all the others whose plans and profits were foiled at the eleventh hour—were found to grumble, but all were rather full of sincere sympathy and anxiety for the stricken King, and throughcut the whole country the excitement was intense. The history of his Majesty's illness dates from Saturday, June 14th, the evening of
LONDON WELCOMED THEIR MAJESTIES VOCIFEROUSLY, AND GAVE THEM SUCH

when a distinguished novelist was asked what he con- sidered to be the greatest discovery of the Century, he unhesitatingly replied: "The antiseptic method of surgery." And doctors and scientists all the world over have recognised and availed themselves of the inestimable boon of " Listerism," as it has been called. Lord Lister has had honours showered upon him. He is F.R.S., D.C.L.. LL.D. ; Mr. Gladstone made him a baronet; and Lord Salisbury, in 1896, made him a peer. Sir Frederick Treves, Bart., who performed the operation upon the King, is the leading practising English surgeon of the day. When tie South African War broke out he was appointed Consulting Surgeon to the Forces in South Africa, and was attached to the army of Sir Redvers Buller in Natal, for which he received the medal and three clasps. Sit Frederick, who received the C.B. and K.C.V.O. in 1901, has for some years been surgeon in ordinary to the Prince of Wales and Sergeant- Surgeon to the King since 1901. He is the author of numerous works on anatomy and surgery, and is a specialist on intestinal surgery. Sir Francis Henry Laking. Bart., Physician in Ordinary and Surgeon Apothecary to the King, has been for many years the regular medical attendant of his Majesty. He it was who brought the present Prince of Wales through his dangerous attack of typhoid in 1891. Sir Thomas Smith, who was born in 1833, is one of the King's Honorary Sergeant- Surgeons. He has long been consulting surgeon to Bartholomew's and other London hospitals, and for six years he was Surgeon Extraordinary to Queen Victoria. Sir Thomas Barlow, Bart., who has also been in attendance, was Physician Extraordinary to the late Queen, and is now physician to his Majesty's household, is Professor Of Clinical Medicine and Physician to University College Hospital.

It was at first announced that owing to the King's illness the publication of the Coronation Honours List would be deferred along with a hundred and one other events, but by his Majesty's express desire it was duly made public on the appointed day—a day which under happier circum- stances would have been one of unrestrained rejoicing throughout the British Empire. It is a long time since such an entirely satisfactory list of honours was compiled, and it is clear that great pains have been exercised to make it representative of the various walks of British life. The length of the list is proportionate to the importance of the occasion which it was to have commemorated, and it contains features of unusual interest, not the least noteworthy being the institution of an Order >f Merit, to which the King as Sovereign of the Order has made twelve appointments, represen- ;ative of the Array, the Navy, Science, Art and Letters. This new Order bids fair to be as proud in honour as any to which a Briton can aspire. There is also to be a Civil Service decoration for long and meritorious service, and a medal of >pekcial design will be conferred upon Lord Mayors, Lord Provosts, Mayors and Provosts in the United Kingdom. Among the long array of names which have been singled out for distinction all are notable and many are familiar as household words throughout the King's dominions. H.R.H. the Duke of Connaught is made a Field-Marshal, and the Prince of Wales a GeneraL Lord Milner becomes a Viscount, and upon the Earl of Hopetonn, the retiring Governor - General of Australia, a Marquisate has been bestowed. Sir Francis Knollys, the courteous and indefatigable Private Secretary to the King, and an old personal friend of his Majesty, is raised to the Peerage, and the whole list does not contain a reward more fully earned or more popular with the public. Sir Francis, as we must call him for the last time, has served the King in his present capacity for thirty- two years, and his tact and kindliness are pro- verbial, is always ready to give all informs-
SOME PROMINENT RECIPIENTS OF HONOURS .
1, ON. H.R.H. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT (Field MSTSIAI). 2, SIR FRANCIS KNOLLS (Peerage). 3, LORD MILNER (Viscounty). 4, me kowean POTNTER, (Baronetcy).
5, R. CONIN DOYLE (Knighthood). 6, THE EARL or
HOPETOUN (MS.PqßiSate). -7, SIR HUBERT PARRY, XITS.DOC. (Baronetcy). 8, MR. CHARLES WYADHAM (Knighthood).

- - lion at his disposal, and his popularity with all about the Court is immense. With the one exception of the King himself, he is probably the most hard-worked man in Europe, and certainly he is not the least obliging. Another exceedingly popular distinction is the knighthood conferred upon Dr. Conan Doyle, who will henceforth is all Likelihood be familiarly known as Sir Sherlock Holmes. The honours which have been bestowed upon his Majesty's medical attendants are referred to elsewhere, and are eloquent of our Sovereign's unfailing thoughtfulness, and the keen interest which he has always taken in the advances of medicine and surgery. The claims of Art and Music have not been overlooked. Sir Edward Poynter, the talented President of the Royal Academy, and Sir Hubert Parry, the famous composer, are both made baronets, and other well-known artists and musicians have been suitably honoured. The Drama does not go without a laurel either, for a knight- hood is conferred upon Mr. Charles Wyndham, who if he has done less for the Stage in its higher artistic developments than Mr. Tree and some others, is, from his charitable efforts, fully entitled to an honour which personal popularity fully con- firms. Did space permit numerous other eminent names might be selected from the list for special reference, but suffice it to say that every one of the honours which have been bestowed is richly deserved. Seldom has an Honours -List been se favourably received. The usual expressions of disappointment and dissatisfaction have been almost absent on this occasion, which is anothet Illustration of his Majesty's wonderful tact Lunt remarkable Dowers o 4 discrimMatioa.

div.p: REDUCED FACSIMILE OF' THE EXTRAORDINARY
ISSUE OF THE " GAZETTE " CONTAINING THE OFFICIAL ANNOUNCEMENT OF THE KING'S
ILLNESS.

the great military tattoo at Aldershot preparatory to the big review on Laffan's Plain on the Monday, the first of the Coronation festivities, when it will be remembered, that the King returned to the Royal Pavilion in great pain, and sent for Sir Francis Laking from town in the middle of the night. After a quiet Sunday he was fit to drive to Windsor on the Monday, and there, instead of going to Ascot, he spent a very quiet week, nursing his strength for the trying ordeal before him. On the Monday following the King and Queen arrived in town, and drove amidst vociferous crowds from Paddington to Buckingham Palace, his Majesty looking anything but weld and healthy. He was too fatigued to pre- side in the evening over the great dinner to the Royal guests; and upon the Tuesday morning he was in such great pain that an immediate consulta- tion was held between Lord Lister, Sir Thomas Smith, Sir Frederick Treves, Sir Thomas Barlow, and Sir Francis Laking, who decided that his Majesty was suffering from perityphlitis, and must at once be operated upon. By eleven in the morning the fiat had gone forth that the Coronation was indefinitely postponed, and by 2 p.m. a bulletin was posted outside the Palace announcing that the operation had been carried out most successfully. Naturally the public anxiety was intense, and conse- quently the issue of bulletins was frequent, but it is a happy fact to record that, up to the time of writing, each one has been fully satisfactory. At first it was feared that the hope of the King's recovery was somewhat remote, but row we have every reason to believe that in a few iveeks he will once more be restored to his usual robust health, and that 1902 will, after all, see his Coronation. The blow was a bitter one to everyone—to none more than the King himself—and the anxiety has been very great, but now it looks as though the worst is past.

During the trying period of suspense through which we have been passing, public interest has naturally been directed towards the eminent medical men who have been attending the King since the out- set of his illness, and upon whose skill so much depended. It afforded the nation much gratifica- tion to find that the names of three of them— Lord Lister, Sir Frederick Treves, and Sir Francis Laing appeared in the Honours List, Lord

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JULY 4th. 192.

THE news that the lallo From Fear to is "out of immediate danger," Hope. confirmed as it is by the daily bulletins which have followed it, has turned the attitude of the nation from fear to hope. There was something so astounding and so crushing in the first intimation that it was natural to exagger- ate the actual danger, and to anticipate from a catastrophe so tragic an issue which fitted the gloomy prelude. It read like the opening of some ancient parable designed to teach us the vanity, of all mortal things and the frailty of human glory. But these melancholy impressions have passed. They were, after all, no more than the emotions of the awe-stricken spectator. The real facts are less appalling and more comforting. The pageant has been postponed '; but that, after all, is a trifle, and, while one regrets that the poor and the young should miss the simple pleasure of a gorgeous spectacle, this new love for the pomp and trappings of Empire is not the most healthy feature in our national life. A similar taste for the theatrical aspects of power was one of the oarliest symptoms of Roman decadence. Oar Continental neighbours used to laugh at our in- 3ensibility to these external things. Now they point in amazement to the new zest with which we have learnt to " maffick." But, on the whole, if the King passes safely through the tedious phases of a long convalescence, the painful experience will not be without gain both for him and for his sub- jects. We have learnt to know him better. Pluck and thoughtfulness are two qualities which we cannot praise too highly, and undoubtedly he has shewn both. Rather than disappoint the people of the promised festival he was willing to endure great agony and serious risk. His first thought through all these weeks has been the duty which lay before him, and the pleasure which he hoped to give to his subjects. Nothing could do more to deepen loyalty than a knowledge of these qualities.

LIKE the previous enrts The New of this Government to solve Education Bill, the Education problem, the present Education Bill has broken down midway In its lame career. It has not been abandoned like its predecessors—it has been reconstructed. The improvements, however, are solely designed to satisfy the loyal country Tory. Nothing has been done to meet the criticisms of the Opposi- tion, and the eighty Unionist, Nonconformist, and Low Church members who had signed a protest against some of its clauses are treated as traitors who can be voted down when the time comes with Irish Catholic votes. The Bill in its new shape does nothing whatever to secure or even to encour- age efficiency, and it leaves the old clauses which did so little to secure public control over the new rate-aided and tax-aided clerical schools absolutely untouched. It does,however,meet the Objections of those rani Tories who,after devoting their:careers to opposing School Boards,felt that it would be a sorryiend,to so much consistent selfish- ness if a rate were, after all to ho levied on their estates for the maintenance of their own sectarian schools. Even under the new Bill SMIIO nomina 1 rate is still inevitable, but there is to be a dole of nearly two:millions annually from the Exchequer to subsidise clerical and "necessitous" Board S3bools. It is not clear why districts which have shewn self- sacrifice and zeal, and maintain excellent Board Schools, should go empty away while the favours of the State are lavished on localities too indolent or too close-fisted to taN themselves for the edu- cation of their children. But, after all, it matters comparatively little to Liberals how the money is found. Our position is that public expenditure Must be subjected to public control, and for this the revised Bill makes no more provision than did its unregenerate predecessers.
At the Cape.
A month of peace has done little to relax the severity of he South

African censorship. It is significant, for example that the news of the King's illness was withheld even from Johannesburg for two days after the telegram arrived. The prevailing idea in such " news " as reaches us is apparently to persuade us thatlthe Boers positively:enjoyed being conquered, that they surrendered their independence with something akin to enthusiasm, and that their only ambition now is to vie with us in an extravagant 103,8.43 . If we are unlucky enough to creJit these .stions we shall fall anew into our old mis calcula- tions. Things have gone so far that the " Times "
I

has solemnly assured ns—(l) that General Botha said the day on which he surrendered was the happiest in his life,and (2) that he hoped the Cape Constitution woulditbe suppressed. Needless to say, bo,th tales are false, and General Bortra. has himself contradicted them with some indignation. The fact is, of course, that the Boers surrendered to force. If they become loyal citizens their loyalty will rest not on sentiment but on calcula- tion. They are pra.2tical men, and realise that if we behave fairly it is better to co-operate with us than to Lister an eternal race fued. But if we forget this plain fact, and presume on their "loyalty," a rude awakening awaits us. And that will happen swift!y enough if the present semi- official agitation for the destruction of the Cape Constitution is allowed to go much farther. It was the late Mr CECIL RHODES who started it. Dr JAmEsox is carrying it ou, and he has no.,v per- suaded forty-two Caps members to side with him. These gentlemen wrote to Lord MILKER for his 'opinion. He replied, "unofficially," warmly ap. proving their policy. His letter has been published and it is vain for his friends to plead that it is unofficial. A letter from a High Commissioner to forty-two members of Parliament is a public document. A more unconstitutional move was never taken by a Colonial Governor. Lord MILNER is not a party leader. He is the repre- sentative of the KING. What would be said if the King were to write to forty-two Liberal members opposing the Bread Tax, or to forty-two Tories recommending the Education Bill? Lord MILNER is trying to force the hand both of the Cape and the Imperial Government, to play the autocrat, I much as he did in 1899, when a Dutch Ministry was striving to avert a war. His action is the more inexcusable because two years ago he gave an explicit promise in a public proclamation that the Constitution should not be tampered with. There is no room in our Colonies for a dictator. We shall either have to find some other sphere for his talents, or make up our minds to the per- manent alienation not merely of the Cape Dutch- men, but of the whole Dutch race in South Africa.

Some amusing and not uninstructive collections are being made of accounts and pictures by enter- prising and imaginative journalists and artists of the:Coronation ceremonies which have not taken place. One part of these collections is praise- worthy enough. It consists of pictures which were confessedly produced, and, indeed, offered to the public, weeks or months before the events por- trayed were arranged to take place. Everyone has seen the large coloured prints—not without their degree of artistic merit—representing the Coronation; but in the general way those responsible for their production have nothing to excuse or explain. It is rather different with some of those publica- tions which, though printed in advandb,bear dates after that of the ceremony, and which were not content with giving a mere programme of the ceremony, but commented on it as a thing of the past. In what is, perhaps, the worst instance the ceremony is supposed to be described by "A Peer's Daughter," who tells her readers that" the Coro- nation was a wonderful sight—for those inside the Abbey, at all events," and who describes also in gushing language "the Procession next day." There is as bad as this in an account of the " Gala Night at the Opera," where the artistes in the per- formance which never took place are severely criticised. Making every allowance for the diffi- culties of society journalism, it is a lamentable performance. One or two apologies to dis- tinguished singers, if not to the public, seem distinctly called for.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
---- A Provincial Letter. \

No class of persons has more natural and sub- stantial reason for vexation and disappointment over the Coronation crisis than that of certain inmates of his Majesty's Prisons. The Government have but little to do with the decision as to how these individuals have to be treated during the still " on-coming "period of universal rejoicing ; though many of them had some foretaste of it in the dinners already promised and provided accordingly, last week. The matter is one in which the Sovereign is directly concerned, and his Nlajesty is said to have,indicated his desire to exercise, as far as is consistent with the public weal, his preroga- tive of mercy. Previous to the sad occurrence of Tuesday, the 24th ult.. a Royal decree had been issued regarding military offenders. It was then understood that in cases of minor offending, sen- tences would be remitted, and that in others of a more serious character allowances of time would be made. If this extension of the Royal clemency still remains good, and there is reason to believe it, does, it will, of course, be greatly appreciated. For it will bring joy and gladness not only to the offsn- dors themselves, but into the homes and families from which they have been temporarily removed on account of possibly unpremeditated misdemean- ours. But the question of how far the Royal clem- ency to the inmates of our civil penal establish- ments really ought to be carried is wide and com- plex. The suggestion of a general amnesty is. of course, absurd ; for the idea of letting loose habitual criminals on Society, at a time of general rejoicing, would be like liberating them first and then placing such temptations in their wa3, as they were scarcely likely to resist, and would thus lead nem back almost immediately to their old quarters. The more reasonable supposition is that, whenever the Coronation does take place, • the sen- tences of the gmajority of those suffer- ing imprisonment and penal servitude may be somewhat curtailed, as special marks of the King's clemency. But, under any circumstances, certain prisoners have especial and good personal reasons for regretting the King's indisposition, and that it should have happened just when it did.

''Tis an ill wind that blows no good to any- body," and the wind that was ill for King Uward, and bad for the nation at large, was calculated to bring good at least for architects and builders. When his Majesty's health is re-established, as we are all praying it speedily may be, the stands innumerable and structures of all kinds prepared for the Coronation, will have to be erected afresh ; since the emerging from his great and unexpected trial, at such a time as that which had ben con- templated. will make the people more enthusiastic- ally loyal to the King than ever, and more bent upon a suitable welcome and witnessing a grand historic procession, if architects and builders are not unduly elated at the prospect, and too pleased with themselves to accept a hint, it might be sug- gested that they should endeavour to profit by the experience of the past in such a way as to avoid some of the mistakes that were heard of from cer- tain towns in the provinces two or three weeks since. These complaints did not refer merely to the flimsiness of some of the structures—this is a Point which the local surveyors usually have an eye upon—but to arrangements by which the approaches to seats already paid for were not only dangerous, but otherwise objectionable to the ladies for whom they were intended. Some regard should also be had to the possibilities of the weather and its pro- bable effects upon the:seatholders.

Yet Stanmore one day last week. vro by Lord ;lit enev.er the Coronation takes place the present Prince of Wales will be the first of his rank to attend such i tion. It seems surprising, yet every echoollbofyanC. or schoolgirl is in a position to know by a little re- flection that this is actually the case. div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JULY 4, 1902

That Turkey is an outlying part of Asia in Europe has been brought hcme to some of us this week in striking fashion. English cricket teams, it appears, have been accustomed to play on a space outside Consiantinople,but are henc,forth for- bidden to do so, for a very Turkey-like kind of reason. The Porte regards the concourse of people as "undesirable." To English minds it is incon- ceivable that international complications should arise out of a game of cricket, but to the mind of a Tark itis " as clear as mad,' to use a Yankeeism. Still it is hard that Englis.h cricketers should lose their sport because Turkish officials are afflicted with a species of idiocy. There is one consolation, truly, and that is that if we must hare another quarrel with the Suitan,we shall belall Jingoes then There will be no division between Tories sni Radicals ; for both will be alike delighted at the prospect of coercing Abdul and his myrmidons in favour of cricket while, as for the C.,lonies, they will jump at once into the holy cause of the British bat and ball " Bal," of course, the unholy Turk designates cricket. With a little firmness, how- ever, the Sultan may yet be persuaded to capitulate as he has done beforeand, not only so,but to order his evil reporting Pashas to stand up to fast bowl- ing without pads. It has been suggested that if Mr F S Jackson should contest North Leeds on the programme of justice to British cricke tersiit would be wisdom on the part of the Liberals at the crisis which has arisen to refrain from opposition.

and children, ever seen in Runcorn paraded the streets. For once church and chapel children walked side by aide, sectarianism for the moment was annihilated. It was essehAaPy a united town's parade. Every school contributed its quota, at least two thousand children taking part. Many were gaily dressed in the characters they had intended to impersonate at the official parade. The poorest child looked like a fairy, the richeEt, an angel. Everyone is agreed that the procession was one of the finest spectsc- ular displays Runcorn ever has witnessed or ever witness. It has been asserted that the revolutionary processionists were the reverse of decorous. But this is entirely false. The utmost order was preserved through- out,and it speaks well for the town that at a time when he air was so fully charged with moral electricity that no unseemly actions occurred. Flags, banners, banner- te tee, streamers, baskets of flowers, carried by nearly every juvenile added a pictureigieness to the scene which may be imagined but is, ver portrayed in cold print. Some faint idea may be gathered of the ' dimensions when it is stated that the children in close file reached at least two miles in length. All the time the procession was on the move the streets were ' ' crowded with people who, at times, vociferously ag.- plauded the children and the leaders of the revolt. Fne route taken was Halton-road,Victoria-road, Shaw-street Waterloo-road, Church-street, High-street, and Devcn shire-square. Prior to the breaking up of ths processioa the people massed up in Bridge-street, around the im- provised platform erected by the town's Committee, Mr D Billington, one of the principal organizers, was appointed chairman. Several speeches were delivered, and on the motion of Messrs R W Harrop, seconded by Mr Rutter, it was uoanimo lel y decided to despatch the following message to the fling "To his Majesty the King. The inhab:tants ri Run• corn, assembled en ma,se,sympsthin with your Majest in your present illness, congratulate you on your inc proveme nt, and pray lor your speedy recovery. Signed DAVID BILLINOT3N, chairman." _ .

, The tAegram was despatched on Saturday morning an within a few hours the following reply was received : "To David Billington, Eq., Runcorn. Many thanks fcr your kind telegram. L will b? laid before the King. Bis Majesty is progressing most satisfactorily KNOLLYS.

On the Friday eve Ping public excitement was by n means a Payed. At dusk many of the cbildren who ha taken part in tbe afternoon proceesinn congregated together, dressed in fancy costurnee and carrying gLiw- log Chinese lanterns. Marshailed by several kindly dis- posed gentlemen, the children—vim numbered some hundreds—paraded tee leading thoroughfares, followed by a large appreciative crowd. During their march the processicnists halted several times to slog patriotic airs with a gusto rarely witnessed. ILppily th diver.ing into legitimate, even trough officially irregulet channels et tne superfluous energies of the town served to work off in a proper meaner the frenzy into which certain sec- tions of the people had lashed themselves. The people, rightly or wrongly, were smarting urader what apaeared te them to be a cerise if injustice. D.fferent from many towns, they refrained from violence and exerted them- selves to soften the disappointment of the children—an action which if indiscreet WAS still to a certain eirent praiseworthy. It may be added that the first orgenia i- tion to publicly diaelaiin the attitude taken by the authorities in postponing the children and old folks treats Was the Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porters Association which on the Friday morning paraded tne streets in coast dress headed by the Weston Salt Works band. The probability is that had the autheritiee announced that in the event of the King being pronounced out cf eaneer the treats to the children and olci folk would be held much unnec ‘ss- ary friction between the authorities and the working classes wattle have been avoided. As it was, everybody seemed to be imbued with the idea that the procession and treats were pestpened for "ever and a day." C iii- trary to general expectation, the chiefs of tne ' own denided on the Royal proclamation issued on Monday to proceed with some of the projected fesrivities.Hurriedly enough the lantern parade which should have been held on To ursday was organized and the different day schno's Iturne d out on Monday evening in full regalia te march , to the common to witness the burning of the bonfire. Seldom has Runcorn witnessed so pretty a spectacle. The Higher Gre de Scheel, tne National School, the Board School, and tee St. Edward's Catholic school massed together at 8 p.m. on the Market Square. For once allthe youthful life of th e town met:toeether uncle the most happy conditions. Rarely a child was present but was attired in some picturesque garment indicative of the life of some foreigu country. The National life of England was portrayed in all its work-s-day aspects with great scope and originality. It is sufficient to say there was not a single element wanting to make a perfect representation of the multi- farious life of the Empire. Prior to the chil iren moving off to Runcorn Heath they massed together and very sweetly sang a special Coronation anthem led by the Volunteer baud. The lanterns were then lighted which shed an additional lustre to $ seene which was it once simp'e, charming and magnificent. Followed by crowds of people the pageant wended its way to the Heath to obtain a good view of the huge bonfire erected on the Beacon rock. Shortly after ten p.m the huge plc composed of barrels of pitch and bsulkes of timber„ Was set ablaze and fa a few minutes amid the Plaudits of a crowd which seemed to represent the whole of Runcorn ths entire mass was throwing its lurid dames to the sky. The fire was blazing until the small hours of Tuesdsy morning. By far the best section of the parade on Monday even- ing Was the Board School. The scholars numbered over 700. They were in charge of Mr F J Moultoa, head teacher, and the assistants with Miss Kilburn, head mistress. At the head of the procession were Messre S Taylor, J Pritchard, and F J Norman. - AGED PERSONS CORONATION TREAT.

On Wednesday evening the aged persons treat which had originally been intended to mark the King's Corona- tion was hold at the Public Hall in commemoration of the King's recovery. No: a little interest centred in the gathering and the aged people were given a right royal reception. It will be remembered that the treat was indefinitely postponed by reason of the King's illness and it was only on Monday evening that it was decided to carry forward the treat. It, therefore, speaks well io officials who had the scheme in hand to organize so detailed a movement at such short notice. And it is oaly necessary to say that the entire proceedings moved on without a hitch. As at the annual aged persons treat ticicets:were issued to all over sixty years ofiaged Add to have glanced at the long rows of happy faces of the veterans one would have thought that all the aged of Runcorn had wended their way to the Public Hall. For those who were too infiroa to walk vehicles were pro- vided and the young fellows of the town really seemed to esteem it an honour to assist sonotf decrepit old body to a comfortable seat. At least four hundred sat down to a first-class substantial tea, being about one hundred in excess of the usual average. The oldest person present was an old lady of 98, who seemed remarkably sprightly for her years. No sooner was tea ended than the enterteinalcre, which is slwayi looked forward to with keen interest followed. There was but little local talent, the chief interest revolving round the person of Mr Harry Gill, who is a prime favourite with Rancorn audieuees. There were several encores, and the social was thoroughly enjoyed. A word of praise is due to Mr G Flow ird tor the admirable way in which he perfected al tua arrangements. Nothing was left to chance, and a mote lord-working an I cur- getic secretary could not pls3inly be found. The old folks were aft it ara.rds given their usu:.l quan- tity of tobacco and tea and the medals were pres:oited by Mr Taylor. The piano was kindly lent by Mr Shaw and the cabs were contriouted by local gentlemen and Messrs Booth and Sous. The following wen the oldest persons present—Mary Robinson. aged 98 ; Catherine Eutegart, 93 ; Harlin Herbert, 86 ; Peter Skelhore, 86 ; B)Phla Rovvles. 84 : Mr Butter, 84 ; Mrs Ratter, 84 ; Mary Moore, 81. ; Mary Kurshaw. 83 ; Henry Cooper, 83 Vllllet Barlow, 83 ; Hannah Key, 83 ; Eizabeth Woinoates, 82 ; Sarah Dan- babin, 82 ; Hannah Smith, 82 ; Isab Horsef all, 83. RUNCORN NOTES. - [By e CORRESPONDENT.

I At the Council meeting couucillois drifted into a very interesting and rather warm discussion re- specting the postponement of the Coronation festivities. There were several spirited, almost eloquent, speeches from the members. Mr Imison excelled himself, and delivered by far the most powerful speech of the debate and argued through- out cogently and clearly. Still it must be admitted that Mr Gatley had a good case could he have bat marshalled his facts ;succinctly and thoroughly grasped the si;,ustion. If Mr Taylor deserves our sympathy, none the less does Mr Gatley. On the latter gentleman has loeri laid, in certain quarters, the onus for the demonstration which was neld on , Friday. Nothing can really be more contrary to the facts of the case than such a s:atement. Mr Gatley, is merely a head cflicial of a club which held a demonstration. It is question- able whether the idea of holding a demonstration sprang from his brain or was hatched in some more fertile intellect. At all events it was the men who compo•ed the society and not Mr Gatley who deter- mined to parade the streets. Mr Gatley had to carry out as an c flicial what the men decreed. He did so. And has been wrongly termed the instigator when at most he officially executed what others had resolved. Jr is too apparent that the procession of school children cannot possihle be laid to his efforts, It was the parents of the town who attached them 4elves and their children to the parade voluntarily and not at the request of anyone. The probability is that the NWaternien and Porters,Society unwillingly averted a calamity which disgraced above one town last week. At the nick of time they diverted the energies of a portion of the townsfolk iato legiti- mate channels,wben stronger counsels would have led to the most disastrous results. Few inside or outside the town adequately realize ;the amount of pent up feeling which lay, paradoxical as it may appear, active, yet dormant, within the breasts of the least cultured of the working clas4es. The Viraterrnea's Society certainly cannot be blamed for their attitude.

With the rowdy element none can have the slightest sympathy. Mr Taylor may have erred in the opinion of some but nothing cmld justify the expressions used by a certain c:ass against & gentle- roan who,e chief conc;ern has always been the I welfare of the town. Mr Taylor, Mr Norman, Mr Imison, the Vicar and others who have been so loudly howled at for their attitude are gentlemen who felt the disappoin,ment every whit as keenly as the average workingman. They did not scotch the festivities 31. n of any selfish desire but purely out of a conscientious conviction that the time was inappropriate for rejoicing Those who cannot agree with them should at least respect their sincerity and applaud the worthiness of their motives. Few, however, will agree mat Mr Taylor adopted the wisest course in precipitately announcing on Wednesday morning that all the festivities woad be postponed after his pronounce- ment on Tuesday evening. He would have adopted a far happier plan had he reserved his decision res- pecting the children's demonstration until a couple of days later. Or, at all events, have publicly announced, that the c'Aldren's parade would take place at the earliest moment after the King had been pronounced out of danger. As it was the people believed that no procession would be held until the actual Coronation of the King which might take place any time after three or twelve months. The sacrifice was more than they could stand, and an open revolt waQ the cpusequeuce. Let us ring the curain down, however,aed may it only rise again on a more happy scene with the bitter- ness of the past completely forgotten.

On Saturday evening Private T Dunbebin, a reservist of the Royal ArtiLery, who has been on active eervice in South Africa during the late cam- paign, returned home. His wife had been advised of nis arrival at Southampton, and when it was known that he was expected in Runcorn on Satur- day evening a large number of friends met at the station to give him a hearty welcome. Dunbebin was escorted through the streets to the accompani- ment of patriotic songs. and wnen be finally reached his destination he was greeted with a loud outburst ot cheering. The immediate neighbour- hood of his house had been specially decorated in honour of his safe return, a prominent position being given to the greeting of Welcome Home."

div.head: CORONATION FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE CORONATION FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn the illness of the King produced a pr found sensation. The startling stews became known on Tuesday afternoon and was at first discredited as an idle rumour, and, later, as a cruzl practical jeke. Whole the direful news was officially verified the whole town appeared to be completely stupefied with the &ad tidings. Men gathered in small knote about the street corners diecuseing the calamity, which had .so unexpectedly befallen the nation. Naturally enough everyone recog- nieed that the catastrophe bad a local aspect as well as its wider and graver issue?. Se long as the King was in danger it was apparent that none of the festivities which had been so eagerly looked forward to could pos- sibly proceed. When the King's wish became known, however, it was presumed by some that a modified pro- gramme could be arranged wnioh might meet the situa- tion so that the many week of toil indulged in pricci- paay by the working class and the money spent on decorations would not altogether be wasted. This, at first, was the idea of Mr 8 Taylor, the chairman of the : Coined. On Tuesday evening at a hurriedly arranged meeting it was resolved that the festivities proceed in a limited degree, and orders to that effect were accord- ingly issued. On Wednesday morning, however, Mr Taylor changed the arrangements made. The nature of the illneae of the King being more , serious than at first imagined rendered it necessary thet the town should not move precipitately in celebrating an event in which the chief parsonage might at any mement succumb. But the alteration did not meet with the unanimous approbation of the popu- lace. The Coronation ctlAer scions had been looked forward to by many who had deterthined to have a jollification and they did mot wish to be bau'ked of their festivity by the illness of any King. On Wednesday evening Mr Taylor called a melting of the townsfolk together to still further ecquaiut them with the reasons of his determinatiou not to let the long projected festivi- ties in any department proceed. The meeting, which was held at tie Technical Institute, was a crowded one. At tee outset it was apparent that there was by no means a complete unanimity on the proposed postpon- ing of the entire programme. Many of the schools had bought their food-3tuff3 for the entertaining of the children, and to forego their tea not only would prove a severe disappointment ti the children but would place them in a somewhat serious financial difficulty. The meeting was a heated one but Mr Taylor adhered firmly to the plan of holding no festivities 80 long as the King was insuch danger:that no one could say at what moment word might by be received that he hid passed away. When this decision became generally known many who bad been decorating their premises deeisteid from further decorations while others, resolved not to have spent their money on ornamentation for nothing, continued to lavish still more tissue paper and bunting on their premises. So that Runcorn on the day ' that should have heralded the crowning of .the , greateet king on earth presented a semi-theatrical effect that was positively pitiable. Many of the busi- ness places on Thursday closed as previously arranged. Still more kept open. One half the workingmen went to their work ; the other half roamed the streets. Some of the children meekly went to school as commanded by the Vicar ; still more stayed at home. On Friday the same state of things went on. Although the King was steadily on the" mend" still the chiefs of the town maintained a solemn silence. Other towns were having processions in celebration of the King's improved con- dition. Yet Runcorn was to be " done" out of its anticipated jollificatioa. Public feeling began to rise. Work was entirely suspended. And it only needed a match to set fire to what would have been one of the worst and most violent outbursts that has ever yet taken place in the town. Happily the disgusted towns folk vented their pent-up energies in the best possible manner. A leading chab resolved at all costs to have their projected parade and turned out in defiance of the decision of the chiefs. The people unorganiud as they were, at once made up their minus to join in the parade and on Friday afternoon one of !;...e largest processions, composed of men, women,

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN QUARTERLY
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN QUARTERLY
MEETING.

For the first time the ordinary quarterly meting : was held at Weston Point on Monday last. Very ' generously the friends at Weston Mint provided a substantial tea. At the business meeting afterward the chair was occupied by the circuit superin- tendent the Rev A Wells. He was sup-. ported by his colleagues the Revs H Morri- son and H B Forster with the circuit stewards. The financial returns presented by the senior treasurer, Mr R H Posnett, were considered highly satisfactory, the ordinary income being the highest reported to the June meeting tor many years. The special expenditure at the Halton road House occasioned a deficiency on the quaner. The numerical returns presented by the Chairman and the Sunday School Temperance returns were deemed satisfactory.—The Rev W Terry Coppin, it was reported,had accepted the invitation of the last mceting to travel as second minister in the circuit at the coming conference. It was also decided that the meeting should make preliminary arrangements for the Rev J W Clarke to succeed the Rev J B Forster as third 'minister. The circuit secretary Mr Povah reported in connec- tion with the Million Guinea Find that the circuit in the first instance had promised 1.000 guineas which had been afterwards raised to £1,600. They now had £1,600 in hand and £73 in reliable promises. Only £7 were required to close the fund. It was resolved that the balance be made up by the circuit. The deficit of ..£2O was contributed by Mr R II Posnett to make sp the district total from £t63o to £l7OO. On the motion of the Circuit Steward, votes of thanks were passed to Mr and Mrs Morri- son for their labours in the circuit.

Application against a Warrington Company, At the Assize Courts. Manchester on Thursday, before Vice-Chancellor Hall, Mr Rutherford applied in the acaon of liedley and II aterhouse v W A Bishop anti Company, Limited, for the appointment of a receiver and manager. Counsel stated that the plaintiffs were debenture holders of the defendant company, and sued on behalf [of themselves and other holders of such debenture stock. The matter was urgent, as the bank held a mortgage for £5,500, and were obtaining judgment against the company for that amount oa Thursday in London, 90 that assets of the company not coutained in the mortgage were is danger. Notice oi the present application had been given to the company, but they did not appear. The company Carried on busi- ness in Warrington as manufacturers of borax, and owned a railway and buildings at Chiquaia, in Chili. They had a paid-up capital of ..-C35,000, and had issued 9,500 debenture stock at five per cent. Default had been made in payment of interest, which made the debentures immediately payable. —Evidence having been given bearing out the above, his Honour appointed a receiver and manager over Monday next to act at once on the /plaintiffs' undertaking to accept twenty-four hours' notice to discharge the appointment.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. The Rev. C.Finch Closes His Ministry
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. The Rev. C.Finch Closes His Ministry
at Warrington.

On Sunday evening the Rev. C. Finch closed his six years' ministry at the Legh-streot Primitive Metho- dist Chapel. There was s good congregation and special music was rendered by the choir. Aster a reference to St. Paul, the rev. gentleman gave a review of his minis- try, and, as for as he could, he estimated its results. He then appealed to those who had not embraced the truths brought before them to do so immediately, and asked those who had been helped by his words to be steadfast. Mr Finch leaves next week for Congleton, and his suc- cessor will be the Rev Mr Reed, of Glasgow. During his stay in Warrington tfie rev. gentleman has gained the respect of all with whom he has been associated, land his departure will be much regretted.

div.head: Ihe Rev John Yonge and the King'3
div.p: Ihe Rev John Yonge and the King'3
Illne-ss.

Reference was made to the illness of the King by the Rev John Yonge, at both morning and evening services at Wycliffe Coogregatioe,.l Church, Warrington, on Sunday. Preaching in the morning from the text James IV, part of 14 and 15 verses,he remarked that not only were we being powerfully reminded of the uncer- tainty of all things human, but we were being, if possible, still more powerfully reminded of the certainty of God. It was no mere conventional, meaningless, platitude and formalism that made men speak of this distressful national event as " the act of God." It was rather a striking acknowledgment, forced in many cases from lips unused to speak (at least with seriousness; of the Divine Being—a striking acknowledgment that God is ; and that He is ever above and behind all human affairs. The qaestion suggested itself : Will men lay this great lesson to heart ? Will they let God's voice linger in their ears ? Will the King himself do this, and will the peoplo do this? Surely if ever Providence asserted its supremacy it did so now! Surely, if ever the Lord's voice called to the nation, it did so in this event which had deranged the plans, and altered the action of the empire all over the world I—At night the preacher based his discourse on the text " 0 Lord, by these things men live, and in all these things is the life of my spii it" (Isaiah 33, part of v. 16.) It seemed to him, ne said, the more he con- sidered the etartlinz event of the past week, that never had God, in present day experience, come out of His secret chamber, and spoken to mankind with so unmistakeable a voice ! Doubtless every preacher who addressed men that day would seek to arouse in them the consciousness that for once at least, they had been arrested on the highway of life,by a lightand a voice from heaven It was not presumptuous—it was the timest and most respectful loyalty—to,expr4ss the earnest hope that the King himself had heard, the Lord's voice speaking directly to him. Lie did not knew as yet what the Lerd's will may be as to recovery. Bac they mighs devoutly hope that it was already clear to him that if God should mercifully bring him back to health,it would be God's meaning that he should order maay depart- ments of his life other thal they had been regulated hitherto. If the Divine Voice dealt with the King in his personal capacity and called upon him to live an altered and amended life, did not God also call upon the people of these realms to seek after similar reformation ? Was thEra not crying need for reform all through the State ? Was there not infinite necessity for revived and renewed religion, faith, obedience to conscience and to God ? If he (the preacher) did not misread the national history of the last ten years, it afforded grave and manifold evi- dences of departure from righteousness and purity and truth that seemed to call for Divine remonstrances. Possibly this moot was one form of such renew:if. If se, bow well it would be, if the nation would accept its teaching.!

div.head: WHEN DOES DEAFNESS BECOME
div.p: WHEN DOES DEAFNESS BECOME
INCURABLE?

although great advances have been made in the treat- ment of Deafness in the past twenty-five years, it has remained for the Drouet Institute to modify the almosc universal opinion, that long-standing cases of Defective Hearing are incurable. In this rosnect, the report of thirty-six cases cured by the Drouet Method during the past month is truly surprising, as a large number of these patients had been all cted by deafness of long duration and had previously tried other special treat- ment without receiving definite benefit. Some of them, indeed, had been operated on. In contrast with these failures, the succeas of the Drouet Treatment is so great, that the Editor of the "Journal for the D3af " has pebliahed details of these thirty-six cases in the form of " Suppiemsnt." Among these cases the following are of great interest : At the age of 64 years, Mr Horne presented for tree- ment, by the Drouet Institute, a case of long standing deafness accompanied by distreAing noises in the ears, which had bean pronounced incurable by his doctor. As Mr Home held the responsible position of Inspector for the British Homes Assurance Corporation, Ltd., the deafness was a great drawback in his occupation, and it was therefore with much gratitude that he reported the successful result of the Drouet method :- 48, Pence-read, South Norwood. May 29th, 1902. -rear Sir,—l am extremely pleased to inform you that I can now hear quite well. I was afraid at my age, viz., 64 years, perhaps I should not wt my hearing re- stored, especially as my doctor informed me he thought I should be permanently deaf. I shall recommend your treatment to all I some in contact with in town and country. With kindest regards and many thanks.—l am yours faithfully, J. HORNE. In the case of Mr S T Taylor, the Drount Treatment restored the hearing after a welt-known Yorkshire epecial.st failed. The deafness was so extreme a watch could not be head ticking unlees pressed closely against the ear. There was a continnoue noise:in the head, like the hissing of escaping steam' and also severe complica- tions in the form of catarrh of the nose and threat. The co npleteness of the cure effected by the Drouet Treat- ment is shown by the following letter : High Pittingtcn, Durham, May 30, 1902. Dear Sir.—l have much pleasure in reporting that my bearing is now as good as eaer it was. I could not hear any one speak,now I can hear all right. Thanking you for your kind attention,—Yours truly, S. T. TAYLOR.

Those who are interested in reading-a- f-u-11 description of the Drouet t-estment for deafness and diseases of the ear, nose, and throat can obtain a free copy of the " Journal for the Deaf," with a "Supplement " con- taining detailed accounts of the eases cured during the past month by addressing the Secretary, Drouet Institute, Regent's-park•road, London, N.W. WATCH COMMITTEE. MAGISTRATES AND iHE "LONG PULL."

At a meeting of the Watch Cmainittee on June 19 h, the following letter from the Magistrates' Clerk was read :—Bornisgh Magistrates' Clerk'a Office, Warringtnn, 16:h June, 1902. In proposing the minutes Alderman R :tarts referred to the acquisition by the committee on behalf of the town of an exceeding:7 important work of art painted by Mr Henry Woods. They had been anxious for some time to acquire one of Mr Wood' works for many ' reasons. First of all, because hs was a townsman and because his eminent position in the world of art reflected great credit upon the two. He thought the Council would be glad to know that as a result of their negotia- tions with Mr Woods, commenced ai or 3 years ago, what some of them considered perhaps the finest work in this year's academy would become the property of the Corporation. The picture had been warmly admired by competent critics and would be in their possession at the end of the first weAr in August. As the curl is taken out of a feather by damp, so the birtue Is taken out of tea by imperfe-tt or no packing. Let atmospheric influences in upon tea and its nature quickly evaporates. The soul and essence of the leaf vanish. No matter how good a tea may be to begin with, it becomes poor by exposure,to climatic changes. This is why

The committee hoped that the reduction would tend to promote an increased consumption of current and in that way the Corporation would not Buffer any loss in income because tbe additional amount I would probably more than eqoal the reduction in charges. Tbe conceeiou really consisted in a reduc- tion of the limit from I.i hours to 1 hour per day. The reduction would benefit the large consumers mostly. CORPORATION EMPLOYEES, THE FAIR WAGE CLAUSE IMPORTANT RESOLUTION.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, a letter was read from the Amalgamated Society of Car- penters and Joiners, and a further letter ' was read from the Warringtou Trades and Labour Council, on the I question of the fair wage clause in contracts with the Corporation. It was resolved that the following cliuse be iaserted in all future contracts :—"The Conirsctors shall pay all persons engaged or employed by them on the work, the rates of wages recognised in the distriet and shall observe such hours of labour as are genet. Illy accepted as fair in each trade, and shall !from time to time whenever required so to do by the Council. orc- dace to them such evidence as they may deem sufficient that they are paving such wagee and observing such hour!." The following resolution was also passed : " That In the event of any cliff -ranee or dispute arising between any section of the employees of the Corporation and any Committee of the Council, and in the cvent of , such difference or dispute not having been settled by , personal intercourse between the employees and the Commitsee cone rned, the employees shall have the option of being represented in subsequent interviews I by such person or persons as they may appoint." Toe Mayon moved the confirmation of the minut9s.

- Councillor JAMES EVANS, in referring to his action at the last Council meeting when he introduced a motion oa behalf of the Trades and Labour Council, said be took objection to any alteration of the resolution because he was not free to amend or withdraw anything in the original resolution. He desired now to give notice of motion that if the resolution beers them was not satis- factory to the Trades and Labour Council, he would re-introduce the Subj tot and propose the original resolution. Alderman ROBERTS Sjl be desired to say a word Or two which would remove a misunderstanding which existed, he knew, in the minds of certain labour men as to what the purport and intention of the resolution was. There were two ideas present in the minds of the persons who suggested the adoption of the resolution which was discussed at the last meet- in. The first one was that it should be impossible for any man or any body of men who might be selected by their colleague; to represent their demands or requests be fore any,committee,to;suffer in any shape or form because they were Ch., mouth-pieces of their fello;e-workmen . He did not think there was any member of the Corpora- tion who was not prepared to prevent any such thing happening. D /ring the last few months statements had been made that such things had happened, but these statements had not been made definite in character and he did not think it was fair to assume that the state- ments were absolutely correct because they were in cir- culation. They must hold their judgment in suspense until they had the whole facts before them.So far as any- thing could be done to rid the mind of any workingman in the Corporation's employ of any fear of punishment in any way or shape for any activity in any difference or dispute on behalf of his fellows, it ought to be accom- plished. In regard to that, public opinion itself was too strong to make it possible for a public body, which was sent thcre by its constituents and was responsible to them for its actions, to exercise this form of tyranny. There were some who were still of opinion that the resolution before the Council did not in any way im- prove the position of the employ 6. He thought he could show that it did. Under present conditions if any body of men apply for any alteration in their conditions of employment, and the application is refused, the matter is at an end and they can either continue or leave their employment. There was no standing order or resolution by which any committee of the Corporation could be compelled to listen to a statement of the case from any man specially selected by the men affectsd. Under the resolution now proposed, if persona/ negotiations had failed to bring about a settlement, the men bad the right and the com- mittee had no power to refuse to continue Clime uegotia- tions by being represented by anyone whom they may appoint. He considered that a distinct recognition of the principle involved in the resolution which was origin- ally proposed. He trusted that this proposal would to a certain extent maintain the personal relationship between masters and men, which was extremely important to the future well-being of the country. He did not often indulge in prophecy,but he firmly believed that if all the negotiations between masters and men had to be done through officials and officials only, we should have the unpleasant condition of things which happens in America. div.head: BEEORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEEORE the MAGISTRATES
KICKING A PATIENT AT WINVTICK _ASTLUM.-ATTENDANT
HEAVILY FINED,

- At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday. before Messrs G Comber and J Ball, Philip Cameron, an attendant at Winwiek Asylum, was charged with assaulting a patient named Joseph Scram; on June 26th.—Mr Longland, who prosecuted, said that proceedings were taken under see.fion 3iL of ;the .•Luntcv Act' of 186 J, whio i made it a misdemeanour for any attendant to strike a patient. Cameron had been an attendant at Winwiok for some months and knew all the rules and regulations of the asylum. On June 28th there was a patients' ball, and one of the patients. Joseph Scrsgg, was ' standing up. He was told to sit down but became very excited. He had to be carried out along the corridor to his ward. Cameron was standing in the corridor, and while pvising he deliberately kicked Seragg in the region of the stomech. He had soft shoes on. aa d possibly no great damage was done, but it was a distinct breach of discipline. It was reported to his superior, and he was apprehended. Dr Gordon examined the patient, and found no definite marks of injury. There was a alight swelling, which he was not prepared to say was due to injury.—Bvidence was given by John Walker, charge attendant, who said that the patient was under his care. He would be responsible for any marks upon him. He saw the defendant kick the indent, and reported the matter.—Further evidence was given by a seoptid attendant Thomas Higgins, and Dr Gordon.—ln reply to Mr Riley. who defended, the doctor said that previous to the present case the defendant's conduct had teen good.—The defendant was then called, and said there were about a dozen attendants along with the patients. He saw them carrying him, but never kicked him at all —ln reply to Mr Longland. ldefendant said he had been at a number of asylums,and had eft the m for various reasons, such as staying out late, Ac. He alleged that he forgot several places where he had been to. He had, however. never been charged with any similar offence to the present.—Bvidence was given by a large number Of attendants at the asylum, who denied that defendant ever kicked the patient.. -The bench, however. considered the case proved and fined defendant 40s and costs.

A VIOLENT THIEF.—Levi Redfern, a stranger, was charged with stealing a pair of men's shoes value 10s, from a stall in the Market-place the property of Junes Halliwell. He was also charged with assaulting Mr Halliwell in Mill-street. Superintendent Monaghan stated that on Mond Ly Mr Haiti- well was engog lit +king stock,and hal his b,ots and shoes spread on several stalls. Prisoner was lying on a stall near. asleep. or pretending to be asleep. In consequence of information Mr Haltiwall receive i shortly afterwards he went to Mill-street, where he B‘NY prisoner with a pair of shoes. A struggle took place, and prisoner struck Mr lttlliwell twice. Mr Halliwell held prisoner until Police-constable Clough arrived and took him into custody.—Prisoner aMged that he was drunk, but this was denied. This was his fifteenth appearance, and he was sent to gaol for to months. A WALING DAY QUARRYL.—George Lloyd, 77, West- street. was charged with assaulting his wife, Hose Lloyd, on Friday.—Mrs Lloyd.-whose eye was much discoloured, said she had tried to persuade her husband to come out of a public-boos e, and becahse she did so he told her he would give her something when he got her home. On arrival at home ho thumped her, and gave her a bleak eye. He threat- ened to murder her.—Prisoner said his wife was drunk, and that was the reason he assaulted her —Complainant denied the allegation, and a fine of lOs and costs was Imposed. _ WEDNEBDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair), and

.• _ Hutchinson. NEGLECTFUL FATTIER SENT TO GAOL. —Reuben Wilson, late of School-brow, was charged with neglecting his thee children, aged ten, eight and six.—He pleaded guilty.—Mr Crompton, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.CC.. said the pridoner was employed by Mr Unsworth. of Hall-street, and regularly earned 21s per week. About 12 months ago his wife died. and since that time his conduct towards the ehildren had been very bad indeed. At that time he went to live with his sister, a Mrs Grounds. and promised to give her 23s a week for himself and the children. He did not do so. The largest amount ke had ever given her was its, and most weeks he gave her ?a or 48. Mrs (+rounds had togs out and earn her own living and she eventually had to give up bee house to get rid of the prisoner. The I prisoner then allows I his children to go wherever they liked. and Inspector Hackett learned that they had been sleeping out in a stable and were absolutely destitute. The prisoner " subbed " his money every night and spent it in drink. The childree had been greatly neglected and were filthy and very badly fed.—This was prisoner's seventh appearance and he was sent to gaol for a month: WALTZING BETWEEN TRE TRAM L/NEEL —Margaret Burke and Annie Quinn, well-known characters, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on Tuesday evening. Burke was further charged with assaulting a man named John Bdwards. and Quinn with assaulting P.C. Hayes. —Police Constable Stewart said that at ten minutes past ten on Tuesday evening he was on duty in plain clothes In company with P.C. Hayes and saw the prisoners, who were drunk shouting and singing. and making use of abominable language. They ran in front of a tram car corning Along the street. and began waltzing between the metals. The oar driver just managed to pull up about a yard in front of them by using the emergency brake. Witness caught hold of Burke and PC. Hayes took the othor prisoner. When they got in Hose and Crown-street, both the women threw themselves on the ground. The man Edwards came to witness's assistance and Burke kicked him several times about the legs. She bad to be carried all the way to the station. The prisoner Quinn kicked Hayes several times and used very bad language. She had to be carried by four constables.—Burke said she came out on Walking Day and was" .keeping the Co meation up,"—Prisoners were sent to gao 1 for a month.

SALE OF DRINK TO CHILDREN.—At the Wigan County Quarter Sessions yesterday, the magistrates decided, in an apnea! against a decision of the Malroesbury Jus- tices, who bad endorsed the licence of a Charlton publican found guilty of an offence under the Sale of , Drink to Children tot. that for such an offence the I licence could not be endorsed. The Act of 1901, it Was contended, mila' be read with the Acts of 1872 and 1874, and as in the Act of 1872 offences for which licences are endorsed are specified, and no endorsement is specified in the new Act, it was held that the action of the Mal- inesbury Justices was ultra vires, and judgment and costs were given for the appellant, Leave was given to appeal.

div.p: INTERESTING WEDDING AT el TA LATCH FORD.

Bond—Fairclough. A very pretty wedding, and one which aroused considerable interest in the district, took place aS Christ Church, Latchford, on Wednesday afterneoaf in the presence of a large congregation. The con' tracting parties were Miss Adele M Bond, youngest daughter of Mrs Bond, Dalby Villas, Latchford, au,' uf the late Rev George Bond,and Mr J Dutton Fair dough, eldest son of Mr and Mrs John Fairclougi ,of Latchford Grange. The church had been tasi fully decorated for the occasion with beautiful wh' flowers, and the path from the Churchyard gi ' was covered with red baize. The officiating clera were the Rev R 0 Williams, Vicar of Holywell, the Rev F A Screeton, Vicar of Christ Church. bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr ff Bond, was charmingly attired in a dress of white tucked silk, with vandykes of ecru The bodice was trimmed with ecru lace accordion pleated chiffon. She carried a lovl bouquet of white roses and lilies of valley, the gift of the bridegroom. The brir maids were Miss Bond, Miss E Sutcliffe, Dora Fairclough, and Miss Molly Fairclough were attired in white Jap silk dresses with ins• tion over pink. They also wore pink crepe de chi sashes and big black hats. They carried show bouquets and wore bracelets and rings, the gifts the bridegroom. Mr Brereton Fairclough charged the duties of best man. Prior to the vice, Mr Fry, who ably presided at the organ pla: the following appropriate pieces :—" Bride's Mar from Rebekah" (Barnby), "Communion" (J' Gri-on), "Festive March" (Henry:Smart), and "Bridal March" from " Lohengrin " The last-mentioned piece was rendered as the bvi party entered the church. During the service hymn " How welcome was the call " was 87 Whilst the register was being signed, the orgr played "Pastorale" (Calkin), and the wedding Pa. left the church to the strains of Mendelssobli " Wedding March." In the churchyard the nal married couple were freely be,prinkled with fetti. A reception was afterwards held in Parish Rooms,Grappenhall,over ninety guests bel"; present. Later in the day the bride and bridegroll departed :for Scotland where the honeymoorl of being spent. The bride's travelling dress w.as.,(o dark cornflower blue voile trimmed with guIPO lace, and she wore a cream hat :trimmed with ,"to and black poppies. Numerous and costly press° have been received.

div.head: Further Remand.
div.p: Further Remand.

In the luperintendent't room, at the Widnes Police Station, on Tuesday, before his Worship the Mayor (Alderman W W Gossage), Mr Richard Lewis, a major of Volunteers, county magistrate, and town councillor, residing at Ditton Lodge, Dillon, was charged that be being a bookkeeper to Henry Thomas Clancy, the receiver and manager to the estate of John Flutchinscn, deceased. on the 13th day of April, 1901, and on other dates, in the township of Widnes, unlawfully and wil- fully, and with intent to defraud, did make certain false entries in a book—to wit, a cash-book belonging to the said employer, and that the said Richard Lewis at the same time he made the said false entries well knew the same to be false. Mr Paxton (of the firm of Messrs Avieon, Morton, and Paxton), of Liverpool, agents for the Public Prosecutor, appeared for the prosecution; Mr Riley, St. Helens, defended. Mr Paxton said he did not propose to take any mil- deuce that morning. It had not been possible to get all the evidence together to take the witnesses in their natur sl order. It would simplify the case to get a further remand, as it would be more satisfactory than taking the evidence by instalments, and he would pro- pose to adjourn until Wednesday, July 9, at 10.30. Mr Riley I appear for Mr Lewis, and offer no ob- jection to this course. I may say on behalf of the prisoner that at least nine months ago he made a state- ment acknowledging irregularities which would facilitate the bringing to trial of such charges as Mr Paxton thought it right to prefer. He would bow to the inevi- table and do all he could to show the sincerity of hie regret. Mr Gossage : How long will the case last ? Mr Paxton : I don't think long, after what Mr Riley has said. Mr Thomas (magistrates' clerk) : Can all the evi- dence be taken in one day ?
Mr Paxton: Yes. The court was adjourned until Wednesday, July 9, bail in the sum of £2OO and two sums of £lOO each be- ing allowed.

1 A DAY'S TRIP TO SOUTHPORT. i "Gossages" excursion is now one of thisse hardy 1 annuals wnich a certain section of Widnes and Runcorn people look forward to with more than passing interest from one year's end 'to another. Each year there is a remarkably keen interest displayed by the wotkpeople of Messrs Gossage and eons, Ltd., respecting the place to be visited. This time in spite of the Coronation fes- tivities the same keeness was witnessed, Southport , eventually proving first favourite. Fortunately for the success of the trip the day chosen was an admirable One. As in previous years a start was made between 8 a.m. and 9 a.m. on Saturday morning from the London and North-Western Railway station, Widnes. At least two thousand workpeople and their families surrounded the approaches in Victoria-road. Three long trains Isere sufficient to convey the trippers' to their destination,the last train reaching the " Sandhills " long before 11 a.m. which gave all plenty of time for enjoying the many beauties of &putt:inert. To the majority the " sands,' so dear to the infantile heart, were the centre of attrac- tion, the Marine Lake proving a good substitute for the sea which an steadily and persistently recedes from the town. To the more cultivated taste the Botanic Gardens'at Churchtown 'proved a source of unvaryingldelight. At this time of the year the gardens are arrayed in all their finest garb and they appealed to all lovers of the beautiful with peculiar force. The museum, the lake, the conservatories and the places of amusement were the objects of not a little interest and were extensively patronivid by the soap workers. The outskirts of the town have long been considered the strength and beauty of Southport and many availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting the suburbs by driving round the outskirts in the many vehicles which ply such a busy and lucrative trade. The more lethargic contented themselves with enjoying their holiday by sitting on the promenade seats watching the ceaseless stream of fashionable life which constantly surges from end to end. Lovers of ozone wended their way by means of the electric car, down to the end of the pier where some good sport is occasionally seen. All the amusement which the sands afford from the nigger troupe to the switchback railway were in turn patronized by the more restless individuals, and even Kew Gardens and Besketh Park were visited by . not a few. At 8.25, the last train, brought backito the perfumery town the last batch of tired trippers who had so thoroughly enjoyed their " day's outing." It is about ten Teats since Southport was last visited by " Govages " excursion, and in that time the town has undergone changes which have made itconsiderably mere interesting. Owing to the customary munificence of Messrs Gossage and Company, all were provided with sufficient money, asiin previous years, for a hearty dinner.—On the whole a thoroughly enjoyable day was spent. Owing to the urbanity and the indefatigable exertions of Mr Povah, secretary for the trip, all the necessary arrangements were carried through without a hitch—a performance of no little difficulty when all the details arel considered. Mr McConnell was responsible for the railway arrangements, which were entirely aatis- factcry to all concerned.

Mr Allan D Erskine, secretary to the Light Railway Commission, wrote under date 23rd June respecting the application of the Warrington-Northwich Railway intimating that they proposed to make an order in the terms submitted subject to alteration by the Commis- sioners upon their further consideration. Any observa- tions upon the draft by the Rural ilistrict Council oticuld reach the Commissioners before the 10th instant.

Mr Pilling observed that he understood the idea of the Northwich and Warrington light railway was to have gone right from the swing bridge and have been connected with the Warrington line. But when the Commissioners considered the matter they came to some arrangements with the Warrington Corroration for them to take that portion over from the Ship Canal to Victoria-square, and then round by Latchford. Th Parish Council of Stockton Heath had now been given to tuAerstand by the Corperation that they would not pr- ce, d with the scheme as they found it would be too expen,ive to carry it all out. He hod been asked toe request the Council to call the attention of the Corn- missirmers that if the light railway stopped in the cencre of Stockton Heath it would be of very little use to any- body. He would like the Council to recommend that the rally. ay ga right down to the swing bridge. The Chairman : lam afraid it will be now too late. Mr Linaker : Did the Commissioners sanction the complete scheme ? Mr Piiling : This was expressed in the Corporation scheme. It was really a portion of each. Mr Linaker : Exactly ! And now the promoters do no,, intend to carry it out. The Chairman : The Corporation intend to give up that portion owing to the parish of Stockton Heath raising up so many objections. The Clerk said he bad received a draft of the Corpora- tion Order which showed that the line would enter into conjunction with the Warrington and Northwich light railway scheme. PLEASANT PARAGRAPITS' OF course, some achieve greatness, but very few succeed in convincing all their acquaintances that it isn't pure chance. A MAN never fully realises the joys of home until he sits at his own table and criticises his wife's cooking. "WHAT do you think of this new trick of photo- graphing sound waves?" "It ought to hid in securing speaking likenesses." TIIE YOUNG SWEET THING: "I wonder how it is there is no good English equivalent for fiance?" The Savage Bachelor: "How about idiot '?" VIOLA: "I've just finished a unique sofa-pillow. It's stuffed with old love letters. Cody: " rn- deed ! How very nice and soft it must be." "THAT hard-boiled egg gave me a headache." "You shouldn't eat hard-boiled eggs." "I didn't eat it. A fellow hit me with it behind the ear."

TEACHER (suspiciously) : "Who wrote your corn. position, Johnny ? " Johnny: "My father." Teacher : " What, all of it ? ' Johnny: " No'm ; I helped him." GRATEFUL SUBURBANITES.—Towne: "Do you make your cook pay for what she breaks ?" Sub. bibs (in amazement) : "Make her pay? I should say not! Why, every month, besides paying her salary, we reward her liberally for what she didn't break !"

" Looic here, ain't ye got any better sense than to be smokin' while we're handlin' these kegs o' powder? Don't ye know there was an explosion last week that blowed up a dozen men?" "Faith, that cud never happen here." "Why not?" " Bekase there's only two of us workin' here." Silk, Ribbons and Co. are advertising perfectly lovely things at a reduction of twenty per cent." A ecHooL inspector in the North of Ireland was once examining a geography class, and asked the question : "What is a lake ? " He was much amused when a little fellow, evidently a true gem of the Emerald Isle, answered: "It's a hole in a can, sir." "THAT young Softleigh asked me for your hand to-day." "And what did you say to him, papa, dear ? ' "I told him your mother needed both in the washing-tub, but I compromised with him by giving him my foot." " Lor' bless you, sir, we was all looking for you to disappear." "Why, what do you mean?" "Well, sir, you see, the pulpit is rotten, and hasn't been preached in this 10 year or more."

Goon MAN "Do you know what becomes of little boys that use bad words when they are play- ing marbles?" Bad boy: " Yes ! They grows up an' plays golf." "JOSEPHINE iS so thoughtful." "In what way?" Yer ain't got any cakes, have yer ?" "I have cakes of soap." "Thank yer, mum. But I never touch 'em." "JANE. did you break the water-bottle?" "Yes, m'm ; but, fortunately, I broke it into only three pieces." " Fortunately ! How's that fortu- nate ? ' "Oh, m'm, when a thing breaks into many pieces it is hard to pick them all up !"

Suddenly he sur- prised her one morning by eating a liberal plateful and calling for "more." When she asked for an explanation he replied, "I am bound to eat oat- meal till I get strong enough to whip Georgy Scott."

Mr. Scrooge: "But I've heard they've just quarrelled and don't speak." Mrs. Scrooge: "1 know that. They'll refuse, and we needn't have a dinner party at all." INCRIMINATORY EVIDENCE.—" Johnny," said the little fellow's mamma, "I want to give you a piece of cake, but I can't find the key to the pantry." "That's all right, mamma," replied bright little Johnny. "I know how to get in without a key.' "That's all I want to know," she said, as ahl reached for the slipper.

Mr Gatiey said he did not desire to insult the chair or the chairman. Arrangements could have been made that would have satified everyone. The decision was not the decision of the Council or the Coronation Committee. The hands of the society of which he W3B secretary had been forced. He was quite prepared to take his share of the responsibility but not the whole of it. What had been done had been done out of no feelings of disloyalty to the King or the chairman of the Council. He was not disloyal. Tcere were 123,000 children who had taken part in the procession at Liver- pool who were disloyalists too if the watermenwere dis- lloyal.Widnes.Warrington,and larger ciths were also with them on the question. No one wanted to rejoice over the death of the King. Their society bad brought men from the ends of Yorkshire,and Liverpool to Runcorn who were determined that if the procession fell through they would have one of their own. It had nothing to do with the Coronation festivities. He was not respon- sible at all for 700 or 800 children who fell into tne ranks. They attributed to him animosity against the Chairman of the Council. The Chairman : I never said so.

Mr Gatley continuing, said there was no member of the Cauncil more loyal tlyin he was. Yet tney were putting tbewhole blame of Friday's demonstration on his shoulders. The fact of the matter was it was alto- gether wrong not to call the whole of the Coronation Committee together to consider the matter. Mr Imison said the point was that the head of the community had altered certain arrangements yet there were gentlemen who deliberately flouted him and his wishes. The matter was urgent and had to be settled right away. The Chairman did the best that any human being could have done under the circumstances. The Council then rose.
