div.head: MIL WILDING TIIANKED.
div.p: MIL WILDING TIIANKED.

The Highways and Building Committee's minutes which were of a formal character were passed on the motion of Messrs Posnett and Handley. In moving the minutes, Mr Posnett referred to the work of Mr Wilding re the Coronation decorations. On behalf of the High- way Committee he expressed his appreciation of his wcrk during the past month. Everyone in the town owed a deep debt of gratitude for the unstinting energy that Mr Wilding had put into the beautifying of the streets.

THE WATER DEPARTMENT. ANNUAL STATAMENT.

A statement of the income and expenditure for the waterwoiks department for the year ending March 31st 1902 was submitted. The principal expense.; were coal, £452 18s 3d ; rates and taxes, £260 5s ; wages, £5BO 4s 5d ; salaries, £195 ; sinking fund, £564 ; interest £2,315 163 10d total, £5,049 63 2d. The principal receipts wtre water rates,£3,243 lOs id • meters, £867 13s 7d, fittings, £2lO us 4d ; stock. £5OO 85 11d. The year's working showed a loss of £77 6s 8d and a sum of £734 73 8d transferred from the general district rate at 4d in the £. Mr Pritchard in moving the confirmation ot the minutes said that taking all the circumstances into coo- sideration the report could be regarded as satisfactory. They had had to pay an lincreased price for fuel and hey had also provided out of their revenue the sum of £2,879 16s towards the sinking fund so that the deficit of £77 6s 8d was exceedingly satisfactory. The sinking fund from the 31st May last amounted to the sum of £4,902 2s 9d. _ _
llrWisonecoEded and the minutes were passed. THE EDUCATION BILL.

A letter was read from Sir John r Brunner notifying the Council that the Government bad decided not to take their Technical Schools from ttiPrn and place them under the wing of the County Council. He had had a personal interview with Mr Balfour on the subject and had pointed out that in his constituency there were technical schools which bad been given by private gentlemen and that others bad been:raised by voluntary subscription. Mr Balfour told him that he would meet the case which certainly requir- ed consideration and the Government had accordingly done so.

Mr Taylor thought the :communication was a very satisfactory one. There had been much anxiety with reference to their technical E cbcole. There was every aprearance when the Bill was first introduced that they would be takf n cut of the people's control. Everyone would be pleased with the letter from Sir John and the prompt manner in which be had drawn attention to it. No one knew better than Sir John the value of technical schools to the working classes. Mr Posmtt did not feel there was any claim for grati- tuue to the Government at all. If any hody threatened to take his house from him and then did not take it. what cause was there for Fpecial gratitude ? It was a question of common justice. The people of Runcorn had built the Technical Schools, and tbe Government now told them they would not take them after they had paid for them. It would have been unjust had they done 80, . _ _

_ _ Imison pointed cut that the Government did not ask the Council to express their gratitude. Had they done so they would have been able to have given some reason for it. The Government had contributed about £l,OOO towards:the building so it was not unreasonable even if a request bad been put forward by them. He shared to the full the sentiments of appreciation for the action of Sir J T Brunner. Let it be written in letters of gold on the walls of the Council Chamber. Still he did not think the people had anything to lose by the , Government's proposals, He did not know whether it would not have been better for everyone if the institution had been taken out of the hands of the Council and put under the wing of the County Council. They derived a considerable part of their income from that source. He strongly dissented from the remarks of Mr Posnett and thought it a matter which should not have been introduced.
THE POE TPONEEIENT OF THE FESTIVITIES. INTERESTING DISCUSSION. GATLEY TO THE FRONT.

Mr Gatley said he would like to draw the attention of the Council to certain rumours circulated in the town, with regard to the action of the Council in the post- ponement of the Coronation festivities. A 3 a member of the Council the postponement of the festivities, he de sired to say, was no part of any action of his. The Chairman : I may say the Council took no action in the matter at all. It was the decision of something like 200 people of Rurcorn. Mr Gatley : I think, Mr Ctairman, if you will per- mit me to say so; it was not the action of that Commit- tee that brought about the stoppagel of the lestivitka. The Chairman : I take the entiro resp-csitility, Mr Gatley : Thin that will do. Tnat is quite enough for me.

The Chairman (warmly; ; And I am quite prepared to take the responsibility. Continuing, the Chairman said he knew the unkindly feeling brought against him by his action, and he was quite prepared to bear it. Be would meet any argument, and would give his reasons if necessary. Mr Gatley : I take it sir, that the whole action of the people that torced us to do as we did on the Friday, is attributod to my action. Permit me to tell you that it is cot so.

The Chairman : I have not said it was. If it is I cannot help it. (Laughter.) Mr Imison thought it was very generous of the Chair- man to take the en' ire responsibility. The action had been unpopular but he bcped some of them were sufficiently chivalrous to share tht usponsibilits. He had not always agreed with Mr Taylor. He had not always seen eye to eye with him. But he bad always had the greatest respect for him sod had always felt keenly when differences of opinion arose between them. But never in his life had be shared so eordielly with Mr Taylor his views on any matter as in the present instance. If ever there was a titre wheel the People 'owed the chairman of the Council Inya,t- they ewed it on that occasion. He bad teen eats trifle g« wire's,. He had spared neither time nor trot elf, t., rn,t.ke the eere- mossy a great success. And when (i.e ;time came no one could have felt more deeply:tban Mr Ta 3 lor the necessity which arose and which a great many very seasonable people shared,for postponing the whole of the festivities. Now whether Mr Taylot's action was right or wrong he was at least entitled to the sympathy and respect of the people. And he ventured to say that the beet people accorded it him. If a roll were taken it would be feeind that the dissentients were very few and comparatively unimportant. Mr Gatley bad his sympathy. The watermen had been summoned from all parts of the country and it was quite impossible to send them back. So there was some reason for the attitude adopted. Bat he had nothing but the strongest censure for those living in the town who knew the exact circumstances why the festivities bad been stopped. It was distinctle disloyal to the Chairman of the Council if not to the King. Mr Taylor bad a right to demand the postponement and his wish should have been respected. He felt very keenly the manner in which Mr Taylor had been treated. Since then, time most have shown such dissentients that they bad taken an entirely wrong course. He hoped the day would come when they would feel regret for having caused Mr Taylor the pain he must have felt at the attitude of some of the townsfolk. Posnett believed that the great bulk of the pees* had been loyal to Mr Taylor and the decision arrived at by bim. Personally he could only express his deep feeling of gratitude that they had in the town under such trying circumstances, a man who cool take such a strong and bold and righteous stang as Mr Taylor had _done.

Mr Handley said he shared Mr Taylor's responsi- bility to the full. When they were deciding the matter they felt they had never met under more painful circumstances. The time would come when all would applaud Mr Tsylcr's action. If :a telegram had been received announcing the death of the King while they had beer proceeding with their festivities they would have been in the same posi- tion BF Nero who fiddled while Rome was burning. Mr Wilson said that at the ratepayers meeting he did not at first approve of the action of Mr Taylor, but when be had heard his sympathetic speech be loyally fell in with the decision, Mr Taylor was liable to an error of judgment but they all knew his heart was in the right place and he must .command their Sympathy undrr such trying circumstance.

Mr Taylor said "he did not admit that he had erred. If he were confronted with the same difficulty he should do the same again. Let them take his position respect- ing the demonstration on Friday, Fle did not know at what moment word might be received that the sing was dead. What was there to rejoice about ? The crown- ing of the Bing or his burial ? What would have been the result. The very men who had tried to parade the town would have been the first to have bated him.
Mr Gatley (interrupiog) : That ut not true ! Mr Posnett : Yet it is.

The Chairman (continuing). They wouTd have called it e the most disloyal man in Runcorn and have con- demned me before the people. But they did not think. It bad been "We must rejoice." He was sorry that ' Runcorn had been dragged through the mire in such way. Be would be no party to it. They had made' him Chairman and he intended to steer a straigh t course. He wae certain he had done the right thing. (applause.) Mr Gatley waa scrry the question bad raised such a discussion but there was no doubt the people would be pleased to hear the exact position. He would not now read his written reply, but would band it to the press. _ . _ _
. - Mr Posnett (with heat) : Read it. It is an in3ult to the chair.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday afternoon.—Mr A R Norman occupied the chair and there were also present Dr Gastaldi, Messrs T Reynolds, T Wool, J Douslas, the members of the Rural District Council, with G F Ashton (clerk), and W E Hough (assistant c'erk).
CON.IIIIISTIVE SANATORIA.

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council, wrote informing the Board that a Conference would be held at Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on July 10tb. at 2.30 p.m. to deal with the above question.
A- TREAT FOR ORPHAN CHILDREN.

The Brothers of Charity, Buckley Hall Orphanag., Rochdale, wrote under date 23rd June, intimating that they had ciccided to give their boys an extra outing to the seaside in honour of the Coronation at a cost of 3s per bead. It was requested that the Guardians assist the scheme on bshalf of the boys chargeable to their Union.—A further letter on the subject was received postponing the proposed trip in view of the Ring's ill- ness to a later date. _
_ The sanction which the Clerk had granted in view of the treat being carried out, was confirmed, VOTE OF CONDOLENCEITO THE KING.

The Chairman proposed that C-he Board pass a vote of condolence and sympathy to his Majesty the King in his present sickness. Mr Linaker seconded. He said they all sympathised with the Kir gin his serious illness. He hoped sincerely that he would recover and would live many years to reign over them. With regard to the festivities he was pleased to see that a great many places had postponed them. He greatly regretted to hear that certain sections of the community in Runcorn had acted, as others had done at Frodsham by showing hostility to the authori- ties who had done so much for them. Such conduct was most reprehensible and deserved their severest censure. The resolution a as passed. THE CHAIRMAN AND THE CORONATION FESTIVITIES.

The Chairman said that since they last met the country bad r assed through a severe crisis. Be could not help thinking that some of them had emphasized too much the last word in the sentence "God save the King " and neglected the first. Their thoughts should have been turned to God, The finger of death, they hoped, would now be changed to one of mercy, and he trusted that the K ng would soon le restored to health again. It had been a terrible disappointment to all but to none more than the King himself, When they reflected on what the king bad been suffer- ing while stretched on a bed of sickness, they would re- oognien that tbe disappointment appealed to him as well as to the people. He was pleased that so many of the places had postponed their festivities.

div.head: VOTES OF THANES.
div.p: VOTES OF THANES.

The Chairman proposed that a vote of thanks to Mr Taylor and Mr Knowles for their kindness to the inmates during what should have been the celebration of the Coronation festivities. Mr Taylor bad given the officers and inmates a medal, and Mr Knowles a box of chocolates. This was seconded and agreed to.

div.head: INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.

On Monday afternoon,at the Runcorn Police Court, Mr E A White, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Frederick Fleet, aged 12 months, son of Eli Fleet, labourer, 6, Chaucer-street, Runcorn. Dr Ormsby stated that be was called to see deceased about one o'clock on Sundar moreing. The chill was then in a dying condi- tion. He noticed that it had had a sharp attack of diarrhcel, and the lower part of the body was ulcerated. He did not think it would live until morning. Ef-i had made a post-mortem examination of the body, and was of opinion that the child died from exhaustion, conse- quent upon injudicious feeding and natural delicacy. It was a natural cause. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence—that the child died from natural causes. MAN FOUND DROWNED AT RUNCORN.

At the Roncorn Police Court on Monday afternoon, Mr E A White, deputy coroner, held an inquest touch- ing the death of Thomas Aspy, a flatman, whose body was recovered from the Ship Canal, Weston Point, on Saturday. James Mitchell, fire man,in the emplsy of the Ship Canal Company,stated that about 9.15 p.m. he was in the Weaver Hotel with a man named Ashton Water- worth. The deceased came in and had three pints of beer. Witness had three glasses, and his friend had three pints. They all left together, and witness went with deceased as far as the Weaver sheds He then left him to go ahem& and Aspy went in the direction of hig barge. He parted company with deceased about 10.15. P.C. Rowlands deposed to being present at four o'clock on Sunday afternoon when the body was recovered from underneath the bow of a boat in the Ship Cana7. It was fully clothed, but was without a bat. de found in the pocket a Walton lever watch, which had stopped at 12.15. He saw the deceased at 9.30 p.m on Saturday in the Weaver Hotel. He was then quite sober. The Corcner said this was one of those unfortunate cases, which were of frequent occurrence at Runcorn, where there was no clear evidence to show how the man came to be drowned. The jury returned a verdict of "Found d' owned."

div.head: HIS HANDS IN HIS POCKETS.
div.p: HIS HANDS IN HIS POCKETS.

At the inquest on the body of •Cornolius Richards, the Ship Canal Waterman. whose body was taken from the Sankey Canal near Runcorn on Sunday last, it wag stated by the finder of the body that deceased had his bands in his trousers pockets when taken from the water. —The Coroner remarked upon. the peculiarity of this fact, and as there was no evidence to show how the man got into the water, the jury returned an open verdict.

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE AT NEWTON BOTTLE WORKS.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT NEWTON BOTTLE WORKS.
Narrow Escape from Death.

On Thursday afternoon a serious fire broke out at the glass bottle works of Messrs C Barron and Co, Crow- lane, Newton, in one of the wings on the field side, and which is used as a store house for bottles,bay and straw, and packing materials,fowing to the inflammable nature of the packing materials the roof at thelfurther end was quickly demolished, and a huge fire raged uninterrupt- edly. Owing to rottenness the Council's hose pipes were rractically usrlesa, and the workmen and others residing in the vicinity set to work with buckets with a view to preventing the flames spreading. The slates were also taken off some distance from the burning rafters, and the timber work cut away Numerous attempts were made to use the jet, /but it was all in rain, as the force or water played havoc with the pipes. About seven o'clock a man who is known as " Sailor Jack," and resides in Water-street was standing along with a number of others on a portion of the roof, the rafters under which had been partially cut through. Without any warning the timber work gave way and "Sailor Jack "was precipitated to the ground. There was an anxious rush, as the fire was burning furiously close underneath where be stood, whilst there were also bears of bottles stacked there and bags of straw. Assistance was quickly at hand and it was' found that he had alighted on his feet on the straw, and thus had a very narrow escape from death, He had a nasty cut on the right side of the face and neck. Dr Walter Latham, who happened to be on the spot, at once rendered assistance and "Sailor Jack " was taken lume by his wife. Another man was rescued earlier on from the fire just as his clothes were getting ablaze. Owing to the scarcity of proper materials the fire was not extinguished until late at night. The damage is very 1 considerable.

div.head: Warrinaton's Illuminations.
div.p: Warrinaton's Illuminations.

On Saturday night, the Town Hall and other public buildings were again brilliantly illuminated, and large crowds assembled in the main streets'. During the afternoon and evening the Vplunteer Band, under the direction of Bandmaster Richard- son, played for dancing in the Recreation Ground at the Park, and froir 9.30 until a few minutes past twelve on Sunday morning a capital selection of music was given on the drive in front of the Town Hall. The Mayor and Mayoress drove through the principal streets in an open carriage to witness no

JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. •

A poorly attended public meeting was held in the Mission Hall, Earlestown on Thursday evening to take into consideration the question ot the comple- tion of St John's Church. The Rev Tlt Matthews presided and he was supported on the platform by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool, Rev J C Matthews, Rev Canon Penrhyn, Dr Watkins, Dr Mouncey, Mr T A Pimblett, &c. Mr T Martindale (secretary) ' read several letters of apology. Mr Thomas Molyneux in his letter stated that the present was the time to look to matters like that. He hoped to raie with the help of his men's Bible class in the next three years, £250, and he hoped to be able to add a like amount himself, making up £5OO. The chairman moved that the old committee be dissolved The Rev J C Matthews seconded and said the old committee was formed seven years ago, and during the last five years not a single meeting had been held. The motion was carried. The :,ord Bishop moved " That in the opinion of this meeting the time has now arrived for the carrying our, of the completion of St John's Church." Canon Penrhvn seconded the resolution which was duly carried. The election of officers resulted as follows : Chairman, Rev T R Matthews; T reasurers, Messrs Pimblett an T Molyneux ; Secretary, Hr Thomas Martindale, Assistant Secrataries,Messrs B&l,Boardm an, Wilson and Rob,-)rts,and the following committee :—Messrs Allen, A Brown, J Bunting, Joseph Brown,H Ander- ton,R Eaton,B Leyland,Johnson,llayes,R Molyneux, J Rylance, sear, R Wild, S Findley, J Kilmister. Eaton, Martin, Openshaw, I Haskins, Makin, J Jones, M Winstanley, R Smith Marsden, Roscoe, Horridge, Spencer, Duckworth, Joseph Jackson, R Jones, G Date, Hackett, Dean,J Rylance, jun, Dalby, Taylor, Hemmings. Clayton, II Wilson,John Sharpe, J Littler, Richard Jackson, S Dring, H H Duke, P Naylor, Henry Tarbuck, Herbert Birkhead, F Birk- head. DEMONSTRATION Or SI7NDAY SCHOOLS AT EARLESTOWN.

In delightful weather the various Nonconfor- mist Sunday Schools of Earlestown and Newton had their:annual demonstration and treats on Fri- day. Soon after 10 o'clock, the various schools began to muster on the Market greund,accompanied by their respective banners, the children carrying numerous flags and bannerettes. When all were assembled in the places assigned them, the hymns " All hail the power of Jesus' name," and " God be with you till we meet again," were sung under the conductorship of Mr W Banton, Afterwards a pro- cession was formed in the following order:—Sutton Road band ; Congregational Sunday Schools, Bruns- wick Wesleyan. Primitive Methodist, Baptists, Salvation Army and band, Welsh Wesleyans, Man- chester City Mission, and Church of Christ. The route of the procession lay by way of Market-street to the top,then retracing it proceeded along Sankey- street, Legh-street, Viaduct-street. Regent-street, Earle-street, Queen-street. Houghton street, Derby- street, and Hotel-street, into Cross-lane, then via Bridge-street, and Market-street to the Market ground. The heat was very oppressive and one or two of the female scholars were overcome. The infant portion was conveyed in lurries kindly lent by Mr gmmett of the Wagon Works. It was gener- ally admitted that the procession was one of the prettiest that had turned out for some time. On arrival at the Market-place, the procession dis- persed, to reassemble later on at the respective schools, to march to fields which had been kindly placed at their disposal. Tea was provided for all and the afternoon and evening was spent in games and sports of various kinds, a very enjoyable time being spent. TRApEs UN/ONT Prcmc FROISt EIRLEsTOwN.

The Vulcan Foundry and other trades unionist employees in Earlostown on Saturday held what was termed " Coronation Picnic," a journey being made to the ancient city of Chester, and a moEt enjoyable time being spent. A committee consist- ing of the representatives of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, the Boiler Makers Society, the Gas Workera and General Labourers' Union, the Glass Bottle M.akers' Society, the Typographical Society, the Moulders' Society, the Pattern Makers' Society, and Steam Engine Maker.,' Society, with Mr David Williams as seeretary'. made the neces- sary arrangements which were carnal out to the entire satisfaction of everybody. Early in the , morning about 340 members of t!]a societies, including:many superannuated members, assembled at the Wellington Hotel, Earlestown. Headed by the Viaduct Band, the excursionists marched to the station and entrained in a "special" for Chester at five minutPs pest seven o'clock. The city was reached shortly after eight o'clock. Breakfast was partaken of,after which a procession was formed, and to the inspiriting strains of the band the members marched through the streets to the Bowling Green Inn, Brook-street. Ttey made a brave show, their orderly conduct quite impress- ing the Cestrians. The company was temporarily divided, a large number preferring to pay a eying visit to Hawarden instead of raking part in the cuetoraary bowling match. For these waggonettes were provided and they spent a most agreeable time in the village. When the party from Ilawar- den returned a procession was again formed and proceeded to the magnificent Assembly Room in Newgate-street, which was filled to its utmost capacity. Here a very substantial repast was serv- ed and greatly appreciated. After dinner the party sailed up the river as far as Eccleston Ferry. It had been arranged to erect a bandstand on the Eccleston side of the river, but the day being excessively tot the bandsmen sought the cool shades on the Eaton side and there discoursed pleasant music until it was time to make the return journey to Chester. On disembarking the procession was re-formed and marched to the Coach and Horses Hotel in North- gate-street. After a brief halt the trippers accom- panied by an admiring crowd made their way to the station. There by request the band played the National Anthem. The return journey was made to Earlestown in good time.and after having marched ta the Wellington Hotel, the party dispersed.

div.head: CORONATION CELEBRATIONS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: THE CORONATION CELEBRATIONS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

As was foreshadowed in our previous issue the cele- brations at Earlestown and Newton were on a magnifi- cent scale, and outshone anything of the kind ever attempted in the district before. 01 course the serious illness of the King bad a somewhat restraining influence on the people, but it did not prevent the sympathetic display on the part of tha various schools and trades societies. The embellishment of the streets and of the houses and places of business were on a fairly lavish scale and the illumina- tions in the evening were quite beyond expectation. Foil wing the town's procession, there were quite ten thousand on the Meines field, the children taking part in the procession numbering about four thousand. The following are the numbers of the various sections of the procession :—Oddfellows 150, Orangemen, 59 Ear!- town District school and St John's Sunday school 2,000, Wesle:an school 900, Manor school 300, Catholic schools 170, Catholic Association 150, Gas-street School 180, St. Peter's school 600, Wargrave day and Sunday school SOO. The polico arrangements had been most admirably made, and carried out under Inspector Morgan. The Chairman of the Council entertained the members and officials to dinner in the Town Hell, Earlestown. Owing to the vice-chtirman's recent bereavement th-) affair was kept private.

In the afteindln the children were entertained to tea in their respectiva schools a substantial repast being provided them. Each child was pre.ented witb coronation nvdal and cup. In tha eivning a P.Sul- technic diadlay took place in the Mesnes in the presence of a large crowd, and a huge bonfire wai iighted on the Vitriol Mountain.

_ On Friday and Saturday eveninei the town was beautifully illuminated and the streets were thronged with people until a late hour. On Saturday evening all the old people of the district Of the age of 60 years and upwards were entertained to tea. Those residing in Elrlestown were accommodated in the Earlestown Town Hall,and those from the Newton end of the township in the Newton Town Rail. An ex- cellent meat tea was provided by Mr Thomas Molyneux, and the old people thoroughly enjtysd the repast. In addition each female guest was presented with a quarter

pound of tea and each man with two ounces of tobacco, whilst everyone received a Coronation d'oyley. A suit- able entertainment was provided, and durin7 an interval Mr W Collingwood briefly addressed each gathering, sympathetically referring to the King's illness.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MRS. THOMAS
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MRS. THOMAS
ORMAND.

The funeral of the late Mrs Thomas Ormand, of " Torisholme," Earlestown, who died on Tuesday last week, took place on Saturday afternoon, at the Newton Cemetery. There were many manifestations of the wide sympathy felt for the bereaved family, most of the resi- dents on the route to the cemetery. having drawn their blinds or partially closed their shops and the flag at the Town Hall was flown half mast.. The funeral cortege assembled at " Torisholme," and there were present in addition to the relatives,and many friends from the sur- rounding district, representatives of the Urban Council, of which deceased's husband was the vice-chairman,and the officials and members of the congregation of the Earlestown Primitive Methodist Church, in which the deceased lady had taken an active and untiring interest. Prior to leaving,the mourners with deep feeling sang "0 God, our help in ages past," the Rev E Bocock, the resident Primitive Methodist minister, and Mr Banton, the choir master,leading the singing. In a prayer which he offered up at the close of the hymn, Mr Bocock made sympathetic reference to the bereaved family. The ser- vice at the house concluded with the hymn " Lead. kindly Light." The following were the mourners :—Mr Thomas Orrnand (widower), Messrs Perry and Frank Ormand (sons), and other members of the family, Mr and Mrs Peter Thompson (father and rnother),the Misses Thompson (sisters), Dr Thompson Middlesex Hospital (brother) ; the Primitive Methodist Circuit Steward (Mr W Austin), Messrs E J George, F Bagnall, W Warden,W El Dale, and other local preachers, members of the ' Christian Eadeavour Society, the office staff at Viaduct Works, the Revs C E Dove an James Matt, a large number of the members of the congregation. The Newton.in-Makerfield Urban District Council was repre- sented by the following :—Mr W Coldngwoed (chair- man), Dr Latham, Messrs J Simpson, W Gilmour, E L Bent, W Thompson, C Cole (clerk), and A Bowes (sur- veyor)..

The last sad rites at the graveside were conducted by the Rev E Bocock. Prayers were offered by the Rev C E Dove and the Rev James Allatt. Those who bor the deceased lady to her last resting place were Messrs George, Bagnall, Banton, and William Austin, jun., representing the Primitive Methodist Church, and Messrs Anderton, Owen, Gooding, and Liversedge,repre- senting the Viaduct office staff. Th.re were many beautiful wreaths and other floral tributes sent by the relatives and friends, most of whom were present at the funeral, Theffollowinglis the list :—Sorrowing ones at " Torrisholme,".Mother :and Father ; Sisters and Brother ; Mr and Mrs W Austin ; Mr and Mrs W Baines, Mr and Mrs Batteraby, Mr I and Mrs Booth, Rev and Mrs E Bocock, Mrs Willie Ball, Mr and Mrs Burgess, slrs Cronaptoa and family, Mr and Mrs J W Emmett, Mr and Mrs C W Emmett, Mr and Mrs George, Mr and Mrs Gooding, Messrs Alfred and Fred Green, Mrs Handyside, Mr and Mr a Jackson and Mr James Wilson, Mr ;and Mrs Owen, Warrington ; Mr and Mrs Ridyard, Mr and Mrs Joseph Smith, Leigh ; the foreman of the Viaduct Works, Newton-in-Maker- field District Councillors, Office Staff,London and North- Western Waggon Department, Viaduct Works. The funeral arrangements were carried out under the super- vision of Mr E J Georee. MEMORIAL SERVICE. On Sunday evening a memorial service was held in the Primitive Methodist Church, Earlestown, when there was a crowded congregation. The hymn " How blest the righteous," was followed by prayer and then the hymn ' Hark, hark ! my soul." The first lesson was taken from Cor. chap. xv., and the Second lesson from Job ii. The hymns " What are these arrayed in white." and " I left it all with Jesus " were sung.—ln the course of his sermon, the Rev E Bocock paid a glowing tribute to the memory of the deceased, who, he said, was a goodiwoman whose influence would net be lost.— The service concluded with the hymns " Vital spark of Heavenly Flame," and " God be with you till we meet again."

Sports at Winwick Asylum. In accordance with His Majey's wishes that in the country,arrangements made for celebrating the Coronation should oe carried out, the athletic sports arranged for Friday last were held on that date There were flat races,sack races, wheelbarrow races tug-of-war, &c., &c., for both patients and staff, the various events being watched with great interest by the non-competitors, who enthusiastically cheered and encouraged their particular friends. Messrs P Walker and Son's Areas Band added very considerably to the gaiety and pleasure of the patients. Mr Alderman Francomb,Chairman of the Committee of Visitors of the Asylum was present, and at the close of the day congratulated the winners, and thanked the staff for their very suc- cessful efforts to amuse the patients, mentioning especially the Asylum Fire Brigade, who had given a very smart and interesting display Of fire tactics. Miss Francomb then handed the prizes to the suc- cessful competitors. NSW PRINTS AND MUSLINS. New Silks, TrimmlnZ and Lace Collars, New Lace and KU Gloves. BeautfuL Variety,"-19. T. An inquest was held at the Coroner's Court on Saturday, touching the death of James Woods, aged five years, who lived with his parents at 50, Plumpton-street, and was drowned in the St Helens and Sankey canal on the previous Wednesday. It appears that deceased was sitting on the canal bank with his feet in the water when he over- balanced himself and was drowned. Deceased's father recovered the body the same night.—A verdict of" Accidental death " was returned, and the jury expressed sympathy with deceased's parents. Local Tramway Company's Oversight. The South Lancashire Tramways Company have only just commenced running between St Helens and Liverpool, yet they have already fallen feul of the Prescot Urban District Council, tbe mem- bers of which, at the meeting en Tuesday night, complained that the company were not observing the Board of Trade regulations as regards speed and stopping places in Prescot, and that they had also given as one of their stepping places the name of a street which had beea obsolete for the last 25 years. Warrington P.S.A. Society. In connection with this society an intercessory service was held in the Cooperative Hall, Sankey- street, on Sunday afternoon, when there was an excellent attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr /I Taylor. Mr S Mounfield, the speaker, gave a capital address, basing his remarks on the 2nd Chapter of Timothy. Mr E Smith contributed, a solo on the trombone,whieh was much appreciated' Prayer was offered by Mr H Taylor, after which the first verse of the National Anthem was sung. Mr Edward Taylor read the scripture lesson, and the service terminated with the Benediction. The Rev. W. H. Stable's Practical Christianity. The following from the pen of the Vicar (the Rev W H Stables) appears in the July number of the St. Chad's (Over) Parish Magazine :—" Being a bachelor, with all the attendant disadvantages, or otherwise, with a commodious house situated in the highest and most bracing part of this large parish, I propose during the summer months to en- tertain children recently recovered from sickness, or others from less favourably situated portions of the parish to whom a change of air and diet would do good. The only conditions I make are that they must be scrupulously clean and absolutely free from any contamination of infection. This in justice to others. They should, however, be quite well enough to go out and play and enjoy the fresh air, and should not be under 11 or 12 years of age. I only propose to begin with one at a time, and to give each one week's entertainment. Marriage of Dr. M. F. Reaney. The wedding took place at All Saints' Church, Blackheath, S E the other day,of Mr Michael Foster Reaney, /si.B. London, younger son of the late Rev George Sale Ream 4, formerly of Warrington, and at the time of his death vicar of Christ Church, Greenwich, and Mrs G S Reaney, of Resehaven, Ulundo-road, Blackheath, and Miss Adele Susan Edwards, youngest daughter of Mr G M Edwards, late Admiralty, of Coleraine-road, Blackheath. The bride was prettily attired in a dress of ivory Oriental satin with Limerick lace veil (her mother's bridal veil), and a spray of orange blossom, and she wore a brooch and gold bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by Miss Flora Edwards (her sister) and Miss Mabel Reacey (sister of the bridegroom), who wore blue voile dresses, trimmed with white silk and lace, with black picture hate,and little Miss Evelyn Tweedy, dressed in white, The ceremony was performed by the Rev. F R Mercer, M.A, vicar of St. Gregorv's,Canterbury (cousin of the bride), assisted by the Rev Cecil de Carteree,M.A.lvicar of Christ Church,Greenwich• The following are some of the names of the invited guests, the majority of whom were present at the wedding : Sir Michael and Lady Foster,Sir Charles and Lady Gage-Brown (uncle and aunt of the bride), Dr and Mrs Herbert Gage-Brown, Lady Jr William Turner, M.S. of (Queen Anne- street, W), and the Misses Turner, Sir Albert and Lady Luppoe Cappell (all relatives of the bride;, Colonel and Mrs Edis' (uncle and cousin of the bridegroom), Mrs Athur Edis, Miss Olive Edis, Mrs and the Misses Reaney (of Huntingdon), Mrs Gask, Mrs Dudley Parsons, Miss Nield and Miss Clover, Mr and Mrs Tweedy (of Harley), Dr and Mrs Wright (of Lymm), Dr and Mrs Roberts, Dr and Mrs Reginald Wright (of Manchester), Dr and Mrs Hart (of Blackheath), Dr and Mrs Matheson (of Greenwich), &c. Crowning of the Rose Queen at Lymm. It will be remembered that the May Queen Festival at Lymm on Whit-Thursday was com- pletely spoiled by the wretched weather which prevailed. The committee, therefore, decided to hold another festival last Saturday, which took the form of the crowning of the Rose Queen. Glorious weather favoured the event, and many visitors were attracted to the village. The procession assembled at the Congregational schoolroom in the afternoon, and, headed by the Lymm Church Band, proceeded via Whitbarrow. and the Cross to the football field. Here the pro- cession, which comprised Maypole, butterfly, Japanese, tambourine, and Italian flower dancers in appropr ate costumes, marched round the field. The Rose Queen was Miss Gertrude Rigby,who was very prettily gowned, and was followed by six little maids of ihonour,:and the crown bearer, (Miss Annie Simpson). The crowning ceremony was grace- fully performed by Mrs Ernest Mumford of Lymm, after which the events of the afternoon were pro- ceeded with. Numerous dances were performed with grace and precision by the children, who had been admirably trained by Mrs Mumford who also arranged the dances. Monsieur Berts' remarkable abilities as a trick cyclist earned for him frequent applause, his various evolutions creating much admiration. Professor Woodward, as a Comic cyclist and equilibrist, was interesting, and the continental clowns, Ribble and Rabble, also pro- vided entertainments. In the evening the dancing and other performances were repeated.
